docs.title: Optimizers in Deep Learning
docs.text: An optimizer updates the weights of a neural network to minimize the loss function.

docs.title: Gradient Descent
docs.text:
The foundational optimizer. The weight update rule is:

\[W_n = W_0 - \eta \cdot \frac{dL}{dW}\] Variant Description Batch Gradient Descent Uses entire dataset per update Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) Uses one sample per update Mini-Batch Gradient Descent Uses a small batch per update

docs.title: Challenges with Basic Gradient Descent
docs.text:
Challenge 1 — Learning Rate is Hard to Set

  • Too high → overshoots the minimum
  • Too low → very slow convergence
  • Workaround: Learning Rate Scheduling — but you have to predefine the schedule before training, so it may not work well for every dataset.

Challenge 2 — Same Learning Rate for All Directions

The learning rate should be flexible per direction — some directions need to move fast, others slow.

Challenge 3 — Local Minima

The optimizer can get stuck in a local minimum instead of the global one.

Challenge 4 — Saddle Point ⭐ Biggest Problem

A saddle point has zero gradient but is not a minimum. Most basic optimizers get stuck here.

docs.title: Exponential Weighted Moving Average (EWMA)
docs.text:
A technique to find the trend in time-series data. Used in time series, finance, and signal processing — and now in deep learning to build better optimizers.

\[V_t = \beta \cdot V_{t-1} + (1 - \beta) \cdot \theta_t\]

Most optimum value: β = 0.9

# In code (using pandas)
x1 = df['meantemp'].ewm(alpha=0.9).mean()   # 0 < alpha < 1
df['ewma'] = x1
df

docs.title: Overview of Optimizers
docs.text: Optimizer Best For Key Advantage Momentum High curvature, noisy gradients Faster than vanilla GD NAG Similar to Momentum Looks ahead before updating Adagrad Sparse data / linear regression Adaptive learning rate RMSProp Neural networks Fixes Adagrad's stalling problem Adam ANN, CNN, RNN Combines Momentum + RMSProp

docs.title: Momentum
docs.text:
Momentum uses EWMA on gradients to build up speed in consistent directions and dampen oscillations.

Performs better in 3 scenarios: high curvature, consistent gradients, noisy gradients (local minima)

\[V_t = \beta \cdot V_{t-1} + \eta \cdot \nabla W_t\] \[W_{t+1} = W_t - V_t\]

When β = 0, this reduces to standard SGD:

\[W_{t+1} = W_t - \eta \cdot \nabla W_t\]

Pros

Faster convergence than vanilla batch gradient descent.

Cons

Can build too much momentum — causes bouncing around the minima, taking extra time to settle.

docs.title: NAG (Nesterov Accelerated Gradient)
docs.text:
NAG is a smarter version of Momentum — it looks ahead before computing the gradient, so it slows down earlier near the minima.

Step 1 — Compute look-ahead position:

\[W_{la} = W_t - \beta \cdot V_{t-1}\]

Step 2 — Compute velocity using look-ahead gradient:

\[V_t = \beta \cdot V_{t-1} + \eta \cdot \nabla W_{la}\]

Step 3 — Update weights:

\[W_{t+1} = W_t - V_t\]

Disadvantage

Oscillation dampening — can still oscillate near minima.

docs.title: Momentum & NAG in Keras
docs.text:
# Vanilla SGD
tf.keras.optimizers.SGD(
    learning_rate=0.01, momentum=0.0, nesterov=False
)

# With Momentum
tf.keras.optimizers.SGD(
    learning_rate=0.01, momentum=0.9, nesterov=False
)

# With NAG
tf.keras.optimizers.SGD(
    learning_rate=0.01, momentum=0.9, nesterov=True
)

docs.title: Adagrad (Adaptive Gradient)
docs.text:
Adagrad adapts the learning rate per parameter — parameters with large gradients get smaller learning rates and vice versa.

\[V_t = V_{t-1} + (\nabla W_t)^2\] \[W_{t+1} = W_t - \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{V_t + \epsilon}} \cdot \nabla W_t\]

Critical Disadvantage

\(V_t\) keeps growing → the learning rate shrinks to near zero → training stalls before reaching the minima. This is why Adagrad is not used in neural networks.

✅ Suitable for: Linear Regression (sparse data)

❌ Not suitable for: Neural Networks

docs.title: RMSProp (Root Mean Square Propagation)
docs.text:
RMSProp fixes Adagrad's stalling problem by using EWMA on the squared gradients instead of accumulating them infinitely.

\[V_t = \beta \cdot V_{t-1} + (1 - \beta)(\nabla W_t)^2 \qquad \beta = 0.95\] \[W_{t+1} = W_t - \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{V_t + \epsilon}} \cdot \nabla W_t\]

No significant disadvantages

RMSProp is one of the most powerful optimizers and works well for both linear and non-linear models.

✅ Suitable for: Linear Regression AND Neural Networks

docs.title: Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation)
docs.text:
Adam combines Momentum (1st moment) and RMSProp (2nd moment) — the best of both worlds. Most powerful optimizer for ANN, CNN, and RNN.

Main update rule:

\[W_{t+1} = W_t - \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{\hat{V}_t + \epsilon}} \cdot \hat{m}_t\]

Momentum term (1st moment):

\[m_t = \beta_1 \cdot m_{t-1} + (1 - \beta_1) \cdot \nabla W_t\]

RMSProp term (2nd moment):

\[V_t = \beta_2 \cdot V_{t-1} + (1 - \beta_2) \cdot (\nabla W_t)^2\]

Default values (Keras): β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.99, η = 0.01 or 0.1

docs.title: Bias Correction
docs.text:
Early in training, \(m_t\) and \(V_t\) are biased towards zero. Bias correction fixes this:

\[\hat{m}_t = \frac{m_t}{1 - \beta_1^t}\] \[\hat{V}_t = \frac{V_t}{1 - \beta_2^t}\]

Here t is the current epoch number.

docs.title: Adam in Keras
docs.text:
tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(
    learning_rate=0.001,
    beta_1=0.9,
    beta_2=0.999,
    epsilon=1e-07
)

docs.title: Summary: Which Optimizer to Use?
docs.text:
Simple problem / baseline     →  SGD
Need faster convergence       →  Momentum or NAG
Sparse features               →  Adagrad
RNNs / general deep learning  →  RMSProp
ANN / CNN / RNN (default)     →  Adam  ⭐

docs.title: TypeScript Notes
docs.text:
Source: TypeScript crash course by LearnwithHasinHayder

These are my personal notes made while following the class. I have kept the original ideas, examples, observations, and learning points, while changing the Bangla explanations into simple English and organizing the material for easier reading.

docs.title: Install TypeScript
docs.text:
npm install -g typescript
tsc --version

tsc = TypeScript Compiler.

docs.title: Needed VS Code Extension
docs.text: • Code Runner

docs.title: File Format
docs.text:
Example:

example.ts

docs.title: 2. Why TypeScript?
3. Types
docs.text:
const country: string = "Bangladesh"
const n: number = 16

const status: boolean = true

If we write:

let x

it will be undefined.

We can see this by writing:

console.log(typeof x)

docs.title: Array type
docs.text:
const countries: string[] = [
    "bangladesh",
    "india",
    "US",
    "UK"
]

docs.title: 4. Run a TypeScript File
docs.text:
We can run a TypeScript file in the terminal using:

node example.ts

or:

bun example.ts

or:

deno example.ts

docs.title: 5. TypeScript → JavaScript Transpilation
docs.text:
Suppose example.ts contains:

function add(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a + b;
}

function subtract(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a - b;
}

function multiply(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a * b;
}

function divide(a: number, b: number): number {
    if (b === 0) {
        throw new Error("Cannot divide by zero");
    }

    return a / b;
}

console.log("add(2, 3) =", add(2, 3));
console.log("subtract(5, 2) =", subtract(5, 2));
console.log("multiply(4, 3) =", multiply(4, 3));
console.log("divide(10, 2) =", divide(10, 2));

Now we want to connect it with an HTML file, so we make an index.html file.

docs.title: index.html
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Document</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Demo</h1>
    <script src="example.ts"></script>
</body>
</html>

If we run this file in a browser, we cannot see the expected output in the console because the browser does not execute .ts files like normal JavaScript files. .ts can also be associated with HLS video-stream files, which can make the browser treat the extension differently.

So we have to convert the TypeScript code into JavaScript. This process is called transpiling.

docs.title: tsconfig.json
docs.text:
Create a tsconfig.json file:

{
    "compilerOptions": {
        "target": "esnext"
    }
}

docs.title: Compile
docs.text:
In the terminal:

tsc

Run this after each time the TypeScript file is changed.

Or:

tsc --watch

We have to run tsc --watch once, and it will automatically update when the TypeScript file changes. Basically, it stays in watch mode.

After this, a new file will automatically be generated:

example.js

So now we have to change the script location in the HTML file too.

docs.title: Updated index.html
docs.text:
<body>
    <h1>Demo</h1>
    <script src="example.js"></script>
</body>

Previously it had example.ts; now we changed it to the JavaScript file.

docs.title: 6. Transpile Multiple TypeScript Files into Different Folders
docs.text:
What if we want to transpile multiple .ts files and put the generated JavaScript files into a different folder?

For example:

assets/
├── js/
└── ts/
    ├── ex1.ts
    ├── ex2.ts
    └── ex3.ts

For this, change tsconfig.json:

{
    "compilerOptions": {
        "target": "esnext",
        "outDir": "assets/js",
        "rootDir": "assets/ts"
    }
}

Now in the terminal:

tsc

or:

tsc --watch

After that, the TypeScript files will automatically be transpiled into the js folder.

We mainly need to set:

  • rootDir → where our TypeScript source files are
  • outDir → where the generated JavaScript files should go

docs.title: 7. Do Not Emit JavaScript When TypeScript Has Errors
docs.text:
Even if there is an error in the TypeScript file, running tsc can still create the JavaScript file. A warning will be shown in the terminal, but this may not be what we want.

If we want TypeScript errors to prevent JavaScript output, we can configure it.

docs.title: tsconfig.json
docs.text:
{
    "compilerOptions": {
        "target": "esnext",
        "noEmitOnError": true
    }
}

noEmitOnError: true means TypeScript will not generate the JavaScript output when there are TypeScript errors.

docs.title: 8. Variable Naming
docs.text:
In TypeScript we can use variable names such as:

  • name
  • status
  • statusbar
  • toolbar
  • etc.

Check naming conventions separately for better knowledge.

We can also do this:

{
    "compilerOptions": {
        "target": "esnext",
        "noEmitOnError": true,
        "moduleDetection": "force"
    }
}

With moduleDetection: "force", TypeScript treats the file as a module.

This can prevent names such as name or status from causing global-scope conflicts.

For better practice, always follow good naming conventions.

docs.title: 9. Arrays
docs.text:
const stdName: string[] = []

stdName.push("tanim")
stdName.push("manim")
stdName.push("kanim")

Another example:

const marks: number[] = [2, 1]

marks.push(7)

docs.title: 10. Objects
docs.text: Let's go to objects.

docs.title: Using type
docs.text:
type User = {
    id: number,
    name: string
}

const person: User = {
    id: 16,
    name: "hasin"
}

const person2: User = {
    id: 18,
    name: "jane"
}

docs.title: Using interface
docs.text:
We can use an interface too. It works similarly to type for this kind of object definition.

With an interface, we do not use the = sign.

interface User {
    id: number,
    name: string
}

const person: User = {
    id: 16,
    name: "hasin"
}

const person2: User = {
    id: 18,
    name: "jane"
}

docs.title: 11. A More Complex Interface Example
docs.text:
interface AppConfig {
    appName: string;
    version: string; // "1.6.0"
    debug: boolean;
    port: number;

    database: {
        host: string;
        port: number;
        username: string;
        password: string;
    };

    features: {
        registration: boolean;
        darkMode: boolean;
    };
}

const config: AppConfig = {}

Here, database and features are nested objects.

We can also create separate interfaces for them. That can make the code cleaner and easier to understand.

interface Database {
    host: string;
    port: number;
    username: string;
    password: string;
}

interface AppConfig {
    appName: string;
    version: string; // "1.6.0"
    debug: boolean;
    port: number;
    database: Database;

    features: {
        registration: boolean;
        darkMode: boolean;
    };
}

In the interface above, we could also use a type instead of an interface.

docs.title: Semicolon vs comma
docs.text:
Here we use ;:

interface Database {
    host: string;
    port: number;
}

We could also use commas. Both are valid, but semicolons are preferable in this style.

docs.title: type vs interface
docs.text: For many object-shape definitions, we can use either type or interface.

docs.title: Tuple
docs.text:
A tuple lets us describe an array with a fixed number and order of element types.

type Point = [number, number]

const location1: Point = [12, 34]

const dhakaLocation: Point = [23.7330, 90.40]

console.log(dhakaLocation)
console.log(dhakaLocation[0])

Another example:

type Player = [string, string, number]

const players: Player[] = [
    ["ronaldo", "portugal", 7],
    ["messi", "argentina", 10]
]

Another example:

type OrderItem = [number, number]

const item: OrderItem = [7, 16]

item.push(20)

console.log(item)

docs.title: Interesting tuple problem
docs.text:
While defining OrderItem, we said it contains two values:

type OrderItem = [number, number]

But JavaScript arrays are still mutable, so push() can add another value:

item.push(20)

This can be surprising because the tuple was intended to represent exactly two values.

For this kind of situation, we can use readonly.

type OrderItem = readonly [number, number]

const item: OrderItem = [7, 16]

item.push(20)

Now the last line will show an error because we are trying to modify a readonly tuple.

docs.title: Another Tuple Example
docs.text:
type Division = [number, number]

function divide(a: number, b: number): Division {
    const quotient = Math.floor(a / b)
    const remainder = a % b

    return [quotient, remainder]
}

const result: Division = divide(7, 2)

console.log(result)

docs.title: 13. Enum
docs.text:
Suppose we have a T-shirt:

type TeeShirt = {
    size: number,
    color: string
}

const t1: TeeShirt = {
    size: 42,
    color: "red"
}

const t2: TeeShirt = {
    size: 38,
    color: "yellow"
}

const t3: TeeShirt = {
    size: 40,
    color: "green"
}

What if the product never had a yellow color, or yellow is currently unavailable?

If we want to prevent a developer from accidentally entering another color, we can use an enum.

enum TColors {
    Red = "red",
    Green = "green",
}

type TeeShirt = {
    size: number,
    color: TColors
}

const t1: TeeShirt = {
    size: 42,
    color: TColors.Red
}

const t2: TeeShirt = {
    size: 38,
    color: "yellow"
}

The yellow line will show an error. We have to use TColors. and then select one of the available colors.

const t3: TeeShirt = {
    size: 40,
    color: TColors.Green
}

docs.title: Another Way to Use Enum
docs.text:
enum Status {
    draft,
    private,
    public
}

Previously, we explicitly assigned values such as:

Red = "red"

Here we did not use =.

In this situation, TypeScript automatically assigns numeric values:

draft   → 0
private → 1
public  → 2

Then:

type Article = {
    id: number;
    title: string;
    status: Status;
};

const article1: Article = {
    id: 1,
    title: "Understanding TypeScript Enums",
    status: Status.draft
};

const article2: Article = {
    id: 2,
    title: "Advanced TypeScript Types",
    status: Status.public
};

console.log(article2)

The status value in the output will be 2.

That 2 is not the article's id. It is the numeric enum value for Status.public.

docs.title: 14. Union Type
docs.text:
A union type lets a value have more than one possible type.

type ID = string | number;

const id: ID = "g-016"

function printId(id: ID) {
    console.log(`ID: ${id}`)
}

printId("g-017")

docs.title: Another Union Example
docs.text:
type Rectangle = {
    height: number;
    width: number;
}

type Circle = {
    radius: number;
}

type Square = {
    length: number;
}

function calculateArea(shape: Rectangle | Circle | Square): number {
    if ("radius" in shape) {
        return Math.PI * shape.radius * shape.radius
    }

    else if ("length" in shape) {
        return shape.length * shape.length
    }

    return shape.height * shape.width
}

We can make the union reusable:

type Shape = Rectangle | Circle | Square

function calculateArea(shape: Shape): number {
    // ...
}

docs.title: 15. Literal Types
docs.text:
Earlier, when we saw Enum, we used it to restrict values to a fixed set.

We can achieve a similar result using literal types.

The enum version would be conceptually like:

// enum Colors {
//     "Red" = "red",
//     "Green" = "green",
//     "Blue" = "blue"
// }

With literal types:

type Colors = "red" | "green" | "blue"

const c: Colors = "red"

This is useful in very common code.

For example:

type Methods = "GET" | "POST" | "DELETE"

const m: Methods = "PUT"

The last line will show an error because "PUT" is not one of the allowed values.

docs.title: 16. Omit Type
docs.text:
TypeScript has many built-in utility types.

Let's first see how we would solve a problem normally.

type User = {
    id: number
    name: string
    email: string
}

const users: User[] = []

let lastId: number = 0

function addUser(name: string, email: string): User {
    const user: User = {
        id: ++lastId,
        name,
        email,
    }

    users.push(user)
    return user
}

Here, we want to pass only name and email. We do not want to pass id, because id should be generated automatically.

addUser("Alice", "alice@example.com")
addUser("Bob", "bob@example.com")

console.log(users)

We can solve this using TypeScript's built-in Omit utility type.

type User = {
    id: number
    name: string
    email: string
}

const users: User[] = []

let lastId: number = 0

function addUser(user: Omit<User, "id">): User {
    const newUser: User = {
        ...user,
        id: ++lastId
    }

    users.push(newUser)
    return newUser
}

Omit<User, "id"> accepts all the properties of User except id.

The ...user part is JavaScript's built-in spread operator.

Because user is an object, we pass the properties as key-value pairs:

addUser({
    name: "Alice",
    email: "alice@example.com"
})

addUser({
    name: "Bob",
    email: "bob@example.com"
})

console.log(users)

docs.title: 17. Optional Properties
docs.text:
We can solve the same problem in another way by making the id property optional.

type User = {
    id?: number
    name: string
    email: string
}

const users: User[] = []

let lastId: number = 0

function addUser(user: User): User {
    const newUser: User = {
        id: ++lastId,
        ...user
    }

    users.push(newUser)
    return newUser
}

addUser({
    name: "Alice",
    email: "alice@example.com"
})

addUser({
    name: "Bob",
    email: "bob@example.com"
})

console.log(users)

Adding ? after a property name makes it an optional property.

That means the property can be provided, but it does not have to be provided.

TypeScript has many other interesting built-in utility types. Study them for better knowledge.

docs.title: 18. Generic
docs.text:
Generic is a powerful TypeScript feature that lets us work with a dynamic type.

Suppose we have:

const fruits: string[] = [
    "apple",
    "banana",
    "cherry",
    "date",
    "elderberry"
]

const numbers: number[] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

If we write:

function getFirstItem(items: string[]): string {
    return items[0]
}

The function is fixed to string.

It accepts strings and returns a string.

If we change it to number, then it would work only with numbers.

But we want a way where the return type is dynamic.

In other words, if we pass strings, we want a string back. If we pass numbers, we want a number back.

docs.title: Generic solution
docs.text:
const fruits: string[] = [
    "apple",
    "banana",
    "cherry",
    "date",
    "elderberry"
]

const numbers: number[] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

function getFirstItem<T>(items: T[]): T {
    return items[0]
}

const firstFruit = getFirstItem(fruits)
const firstNumber = getFirstItem(numbers)

console.log(firstFruit.toUpperCase())
console.log(firstNumber.toFixed(2))

Here we do not use a fixed data type.

T represents the type that is passed to the function.

The <T> portion identifies the generic type, and TypeScript automatically determines what T should be from the argument.

So:

getFirstItem(fruits)

makes T become string.

And:

getFirstItem(numbers)

makes T become number.

docs.title: 19. Generic with API Fetching
docs.text:
Let's see how we can use generics with APIs.

First, define our types:

type User = {
    id: number
    name: string
    email: string
}

type Product = {
    id: number
    name: string
    price: number
}

type Order = {
    id: number
    userId: number
    total: number,
    date: string,
    status: "pending" | "shipped" | "delivered"
}

Example API endpoints:

/api/users
/api/products
/api/orders
Normal TypeScript approachBetter: Generic API function 
async function getUsers(): Promise<User[]> {
    const data = await fetch("/api/users")
    return data.json()
}

async function getProducts(): Promise<Product[]> {
    const data = await fetch("/api/products")
    return data.json()
}

async function getOrders(): Promise<Order[]> {
    const data = await fetch("/api/orders")
    return data.json()
}

const users = await getUsers()
const products = await getProducts()
const orders = await getOrders()

Here we need three different functions for three different types of API data.

We can make the code simpler and shorter using a generic.

async function get<T>(apiEndpoint: string): Promise<T> {
    const data = await fetch(apiEndpoint)
    return data.json()
}

const users = await get<User[]>("/api/users")
const products = await get<Product[]>("/api/products")
const orders = await get<Order[]>("/api/orders")

This single function works for both a single value and an array, depending on the generic type we provide.

Important: Read more about generics because they are very important in TypeScript.

docs.title: 20. Map & Set
docs.text:
Set and Map are useful for storing:

  • unique values → Set
  • key-value pairs → Map

docs.title: Set
docs.text:
Normal JavaScriptTypeScript 
const data = new Set()

data.add("abc")
data.add(30)
data.add(true)

All these data types can be added in a normal JavaScript Set.

We can make the type fixed:

const data = new Set<string>()

Now only string values can be added.

docs.title: Map
docs.text:
Normal JavaScriptTypeScript 
const players = new Map()

players.set("Ronaldo", 7)
players.set(10, "Messi")
players.set("Neymar", "brazil")

const players = new Map<string, number>()

players.set("Ronaldo", 7)
players.set("Messy", 10)

One important thing here is:

Map<keyType, valueType>

The first type is the key, and the second type is the value.

Map keys are unique.

If we use the same key again, the new value replaces the old value.

For example:

players.set("messy", 13)
players.set("messy", 10)

The second line rewrites the value associated with "messy".

So the final value for "messy" is 10.

Because a Map rewrites the value for an existing key, we can use it as a simple counting storage.

docs.title: 21. Practical Map Example: Juice Shop
docs.text:
Suppose we have a juice shop.

We want to automatically count how many times each juice has been ordered.

const orders = new Map<string, number>()

function addOrder(juice: string, count: number) {
    const quantity = orders.get(juice) || 0
    orders.set(juice, quantity + count)
}

addOrder("mango", 2)
addOrder("mango", 4)
addOrder("apple", 5)
addOrder("banana", 1)
addOrder("apple", 2)

console.log(orders)

The Map keeps the total quantity for each juice.

docs.title: 22. TypeScript with HTML
docs.text:
Suppose an HTML file has:

  • one input with id="email"
  • one button with id="send"
Normal approachBetter: Generic querySelector 
const input = document.getElementById("email") as HTMLInputElement
const button = document.getElementById("send") as HTMLButtonElement

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
    console.log(`Subscription complete for ${input.value}`)
})

HTMLInputElement is added because TypeScript knows that getElementById() can return null, and it does not automatically know that the returned element is specifically an input element.

In JavaScript, we do not have to write HTMLInputElement or HTMLButtonElement.

We can do the same thing using a generic:

const input = document.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>("#email")
const button = document.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>("#send")

if (button && input) {
    button.addEventListener("click", () => {
        console.log(`Subscription complete for ${input.value}`)
    })
}

The generic version is better because:

  1. We can specify the element type.
  2. We can also perform a null check.
  3. TypeScript can understand the element type.

So the generic version is generally much better.

docs.title: 23. Project: Task Management Application
docs.text:
Let's build a small task manager application.

Suppose we already have an HTML file.

docs.title: script.ts
docs.text:
First, define the task type:

type Task = {
    id: number;
    title: string;
    completed: boolean;
}

Get the HTML elements:

const form = document.getElementById("task-form") as HTMLFormElement
const input = document.getElementById("task-input") as HTMLInputElement
const list = document.getElementById("task-list") as HTMLUListElement

Create the task storage:

let tasks: Task[] = []
let nextId = 1

docs.title: Create Sample Tasks
docs.text:
Let's create a function for adding sample tasks.

function createSampleTasks(): void {
    const samples: Omit<Task, "id">[] = [
        { title: "Buy groceries", completed: true },
        { title: "Finish TypeScript homework", completed: false },
        { title: "Call the dentist", completed: false },
        { title: "Water the plants", completed: true },
    ]

    samples.forEach((sample) => {
        tasks.push({
            id: nextId++,
            title: sample.title,
            completed: sample.completed
        })
    })
}

createSampleTasks()

console.log(tasks)

Omit<Task, "id"> means all the properties of Task except id.

The id is generated automatically.

docs.title: HTML Task List
docs.text:
In index.html:

<section>
    <h2>Tasks</h2>
    <ul id="task-list">
        <!-- All rendered task data will appear here -->
    </ul>
</section>

docs.title: 24. Render Tasks
docs.text:
Now we need to render the tasks into the HTML file.

Add this after the previous code in script.ts:

function renderTasks(): void {
    list.innerHTML = ""

    tasks.forEach((task) => {
        const li = document.createElement("li")

        const checkbox = document.createElement("input")
        checkbox.type = "checkbox"
        checkbox.checked = task.completed

        checkbox.addEventListener("change", () => {
            task.completed = checkbox.checked
        })

        const span = document.createElement("span")
        span.textContent = task.title

        li.append(checkbox, span)
        list.append(li)
    })
}

docs.title: 25. Add a New Task
docs.text:
Now let's add a function for adding a new task.

function addTask(title: string): void {
    tasks.push({
        id: nextId++,
        title: title,
        completed: false
    })

    renderTasks()
}

Then handle the form submission:

form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
    event.preventDefault()

    addTask(input.value)

    input.value = ""
    input.focus()
})

docs.title: What does event.preventDefault() do?
docs.text:
When a form is submitted, the browser has a default behavior. Usually, the browser may submit the form and reload/navigate the page.

event.preventDefault()

stops that default browser behavior.

This allows our TypeScript code to handle the form submission ourselves without the page being reloaded.

docs.title: What does input.focus() do?
docs.text:
input.focus()

puts the keyboard focus back into the input field.

For example:

  1. Type a task name.
  2. Press Enter.
  3. The task is added.
  4. The input is cleared.
  5. input.focus() puts the cursor back into the input.
  6. We can immediately type the next task without clicking the input again.

docs.title: 26. Script Bundle
docs.text:
In real projects, the entire project script is usually not written in one TypeScript file.

Different responsibilities are separated into different .ts files.

Then we can bundle those TypeScript files and create one JavaScript output file.

This is a more advanced process.

Let's use the same task-management project to learn bundling.

docs.title: Create a src Folder
docs.text:
Inside src, create two files.

src/
├── seed.ts
└── script.ts

docs.title: src/seed.ts
docs.text:
export type Task = {
    id: number;
    title: string;
    completed: boolean;
}

export let tasks: Task[] = []

export let nextId = 1

We could change exported variables directly, but directly changing shared state is generally not the best practice.

So we can use a function:

export function getNextId(): number {
    return nextId++
}

Now the ID is changed through a function instead of directly modifying the variable.

docs.title: Sample task function
docs.text:
export function createSampleTasks(): void {
    const samples: Omit<Task, "id">[] = [
        { title: "Buy groceries", completed: true },
        { title: "Finish TypeScript homework", completed: false },
        { title: "Call the dentist", completed: false },
        { title: "Water the plants", completed: true },
        { title: "Refuel the scooter", completed: false },
    ]

    samples.forEach((sample) => {
        tasks.push({
            id: nextId++,
            title: sample.title,
            completed: sample.completed
        })
    })
}

docs.title: Why are we using export now?
docs.text:
In the earlier version, everything was inside one file, so we did not need to export anything.

Now the code is split into multiple files.

Modern TypeScript projects commonly organize code into modules.

So we export the things that another file needs to import.

docs.title: 27. Import from seed.ts
docs.text: Because we moved some code from script.ts into seed.ts, we need to import those things into script.ts.

docs.title: src/script.ts
docs.text:
import {
    tasks,
    getNextId,
    createSampleTasks
} from "./seed"

const form = document.getElementById("task-form") as HTMLFormElement
const input = document.getElementById("task-input") as HTMLInputElement
const list = document.getElementById("task-list") as HTMLUListElement
const exportButton = document.getElementById("export") as HTMLButtonElement

Then:

function renderTasks(): void {
    list.innerHTML = ""

    tasks.forEach((task) => {
        const li = document.createElement("li")

        const checkbox = document.createElement("input")
        checkbox.type = "checkbox"
        checkbox.checked = task.completed

        checkbox.addEventListener("change", () => {
            task.completed = checkbox.checked
        })

        const span = document.createElement("span")
        span.textContent = task.title

        li.append(checkbox, span)
        list.append(li)
    })
}

Add task:

function addTask(title: string): void {
    tasks.push({
        id: getNextId(),
        title: title,
        completed: false
    })

    renderTasks()
}

Form handling:

form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
    event.preventDefault()

    addTask(input.value)

    input.value = ""
    input.focus()
})

docs.title: 28. Rollup Bundler
docs.text:
Now we have two TypeScript files and want to bundle them into one JavaScript file.

We will use Rollup.

We install packages through package.json, because this is the normal way to manage JavaScript project dependencies.

docs.title: package.json
docs.text:
Create a new package.json:

{
    "name": "task-manager",
    "version": "1.0.0",
    "private": true,
    "type": "module",
    "scripts": {
        "build": "rollup -c",
        "watch": "rollup -c -w"
    },
    "devDependencies": {
        "@rollup/plugin-typescript": "^12.1.0",
        "rollup": "^4.24.0",
        "tslib": "^2.8.0",
        "typescript": "^5.9.0"
    }
}

docs.title: .gitignore
docs.text:
Create another file:

.gitignore

Add:

node_modules

docs.title: Why do we add node_modules to .gitignore?
docs.text:
node_modules contains installed dependencies.

We normally do not push this huge generated folder to GitHub.

Instead, we push:

  • package.json
  • package-lock.json (when generated)

Then another developer or the deployment platform can run:

npm install

and recreate node_modules.

docs.title: Install the packages
docs.text:
In the terminal:

npm install

docs.title: 29. rollup.config.js
docs.text:
Create:

rollup.config.js

Add:

import typescript from "@rollup/plugin-typescript";

export default {
    input: "src/script.ts",

    output: {
        file: "dist/app.js",
        format: "iife"
    },

    plugins: [
        typescript()
    ]
};

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
npm run build

or:

rollup -c

The bundled output will be:

dist/app.js

docs.title: Update index.html
docs.text:
Change the script location:

<script src="dist/app.js"></script>

Instead of loading the individual TypeScript file.

docs.title: Watch Mode
docs.text:
To automatically rebuild when files change:

npm run watch

or:

rollup -c -w

docs.title: 30. Rollup Tree Shaking
docs.text:
Tree shaking is an important built-in Rollup feature.

Suppose we have:

function deleteTask() {
    console.log("will implement")
}

But this function is never used.

Rollup can detect that it is unused and remove it from the final bundle.

So unused code does not need to be included in the production bundle.

This process is called tree shaking.

docs.title: 31. Node.js with TypeScript
docs.text:
Server-side applications such as:

  • Node.js
  • Bun
  • Deno

can work with TypeScript.

Example example.ts:

function add(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a + b
}

function subtract(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a - b
}

console.log(add(10, 6))
console.log(subtract(22, 6))

Run:

node example.ts

or:

bun example.ts

or:

deno example.ts

The class notes point out that Node.js has been adding TypeScript support and that modern Node can run TypeScript files directly in supported situations.

docs.title: 32. TypeScript Modules with Node.js
docs.text:
Let's make the example a module.

Create mathlib.ts:

export function add(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a + b
}

export function subtract(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a - b
}

We can also export at the bottom:

function add(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a + b
}

function subtract(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a - b
}

export { add, subtract }

Then in example.ts:

import { add, subtract } from "./mathlib.ts"

console.log(add(10, 6))
console.log(subtract(22, 6))

The behavior can differ depending on the runtime and its TypeScript/module support.

In the original class example:

node example.ts

was shown as producing an error for this module setup, while:

bun example.ts

and:

deno example.ts

were shown as working.

docs.title: Fixing Node's Module Setup
docs.text:
To fix the module setup for Node, create:

package.json

with:

{
    "type": "module"
}

After this, the module configuration is explicitly set to ES modules.

docs.title: 33. OOP in TypeScript
docs.text:
Before the OOP example, it is important to understand:

  • public
  • private
  • protected

docs.title: public
docs.text:
A public member can be accessed from:

  • inside the class
  • subclasses
  • outside the class

It is the normal accessible member.

Example:

class Account {
    public name: string

    constructor(name: string) {
        this.name = name
    }
}

const account = new Account("Tanim")

console.log(account.name)

docs.title: private
docs.text:
A private member can be accessed only inside the class where it is declared.

It cannot be accessed directly:

  • from outside the class
  • from a subclass

Example:

class Account {
    private balance: number

    constructor(balance: number) {
        this.balance = balance
    }
}

This is not allowed:

const account = new Account(1000)

console.log(account.balance)

docs.title: protected
docs.text:
A protected member can be accessed:

  • inside the class
  • inside subclasses

But it cannot be accessed directly from outside the class.

Example:

class Account {
    protected balance: number

    constructor(balance: number) {
        this.balance = balance
    }
}

class StudentAccount extends Account {
    showBalance() {
        console.log(this.balance)
    }
}

The subclass can use this.balance, but code outside the class hierarchy cannot directly access it.

docs.title: Quick comparison
docs.text: Modifier Inside class Subclass Outside public ✅ ✅ ✅ protected ✅ ✅ ❌ private ✅ ❌ ❌

docs.title: account.ts
docs.text:
class Account {
    readonly id: number;
    public name: string;
    protected balance: number;

    constructor(id: number, name: string, balance: number) {
        this.id = id;
        this.name = name;
        this.balance = balance;
    }
}

Here:

  • readonly id cannot be reassigned after initialization.
  • public name can be accessed from outside.
  • protected balance can be accessed by the class and its subclasses.

docs.title: Constructor Parameter Properties
docs.text:
We can make the class shorter using parameter properties:

class Account {
    constructor(
        public readonly id: number,
        public name: string,
        protected balance: number
    ) {}
}

TypeScript automatically creates and assigns those properties.

docs.title: 35. Add Methods to the Account Class
docs.text:
class Account {
    constructor(
        public readonly id: number,
        public name: string,
        protected balance: number
    ) {}

    deposit(amount: number): void {
        this.balance += amount
    }

    withdraw(amount: number): void {
        if (this.balance < amount) {
            throw new Error("insufficient balance")
        }

        this.balance -= amount
    }

    status(): void {
        console.log(
            `Account ${this.id} (${this.name}) has a balance of ${this.balance}`
        )
    }
}

docs.title: 36. Interface for Different Account Types
docs.text:
An account can have multiple types, and different account types can have different withdrawal limits.

So we can create an interface above the classes.

interface BaseAccount {
    readonly id: number;
    name: string;

    deposit(amount: number): void;
    withdraw(amount: number): void;
    status(): void;
}

docs.title: Important note about access modifiers in interfaces
docs.text:
We do not use public, private, or protected inside an interface.

Interfaces describe the public shape of an object.

Also, balance is not included in this interface because our balance property is protected.

// balance: number

We cannot describe a protected member as a public interface property.

docs.title: Implement the Interface
docs.text:
class Account implements BaseAccount {
    protected isLimited: boolean = false
    protected limit: number = 0

    constructor(
        public readonly id: number,
        public name: string,
        protected balance: number
    ) {}

    deposit(amount: number): void {
        this.balance += amount
    }

    withdraw(amount: number): void {
        if (this.isLimited && amount > this.limit) {
            throw new Error(
                `You cannot withdraw more than ${this.limit}`
            )
        }

        if (this.balance < amount) {
            throw new Error("insufficient balance")
        }

        this.balance -= amount
    }

    status(): void {
        console.log(
            `Account ${this.id} (${this.name}) has a balance of ${this.balance}`
        )
    }
}

docs.title: 37. Inheritance
docs.text:
Now create specialized account classes.

class StudentAccount extends Account {
    protected isLimited: boolean = true
    protected limit: number = 10000
}

Savings account:

class SavingsAccount extends Account {
    protected isLimited: boolean = true
    protected limit: number = 50000
}

Current account:

class CurrentAccount extends Account {}

docs.title: Use the Student Account
docs.text:
const studentAccount = new StudentAccount(
    153,
    "Student A",
    25000
)

studentAccount.withdraw(5000)
studentAccount.status()

studentAccount.withdraw(15000)
studentAccount.status()

The student account has a withdrawal limit of 10000.

So:

studentAccount.withdraw(5000)

is allowed, while:

studentAccount.withdraw(15000)

will throw an error because it exceeds the limit.

docs.title: 38. Creating a Modern TypeScript Project with Vite
docs.text:
Developers do not want to waste time manually creating every folder and configuration file.

They often use Vite to speed up project setup and development.

In the terminal:

npm create vite@latest project_name

Then:

cd project_name
npm install

Open the project in an IDE such as VS Code.

Run:

npm run dev

Vite automatically sets up many things for us.

We can still modify the generated project.

docs.title: 39. Development vs Production
docs.text:
During development, we can use:

npm run dev

to run the development server and visually see the project.

But before deployment, we should make sure the project also works correctly as production code.

So run:

npm run build

Then:

npm run preview

npm run preview lets us visualize the production build.

The preview is based on the build output.

docs.title: Development
docs.text: npm run dev

docs.title: Production build
docs.text: npm run build

docs.title: Preview production build
docs.text: npm run preview

docs.title: 40. GitHub and Deployment
docs.text:
While developing, we normally do not push generated folders such as:

dist/
node_modules/

to GitHub.

So .gitignore should at least contain:

node_modules
dist

We can push the whole source project to GitHub.

Then on a deployment platform:

  1. Log in with GitHub.
  2. Add a new project.
  3. Select the repository.
  4. Deploy.

For example, Vercel can automatically build and deploy the project.

docs.title: 41. Fetch API Data with a Button
docs.text:
Suppose we have a button with the ID btn.

const btn = document.getElementById("btn") as HTMLButtonElement

// const heading = document.getElementById("heading") as HTMLHeadingElement

let data = []

btn.addEventListener("click", async () => {
    const response = await fetch(
        "https://tsapidemo.lwhh.org/api/v1/books"
    )

    const books = await response.json()

    console.log(books)

    data = books

    printBookDetails(books[1])
})

Function:

function printBookDetails(book) {
    // console.clear();

    console.log("ID:", book.id)
    console.log("Title:", book.title)
    console.log("Author:", book.author)
    console.log("Category:", book.category)
    console.log("Price:", book.price)
}

docs.title: What did we do?
docs.text:
First, we fetched data from the API URL.

Then we converted the response into JSON and stored it in books.

Then:

printBookDetails(books[1])

passes one book to the function, so we can see that book's information.

docs.title: 42. Why Validate API Data?
docs.text:
There is a problem.

What if, in the future, someone adds a book with a different key-value structure?

What if there are multiple categories?

What if another key is added?

Our code assumes that the API response always has the exact structure we expect.

So whenever we use API data, we should validate the data to make sure it has the format we expect.

For data validation, we can use a library called Zod.

docs.title: Install Zod
docs.text:
In the terminal:

npm install zod

After installing it, import Zod:

import { z } from "zod"

Importing Zod alone is not enough.

We also need to create a schema describing the format we expect from the API.

docs.title: Book Schema
docs.text:
const BookSchema = z.object({
    id: z.number(),
    title: z.string(),
    author: z.string(),
    category: z.string(),
    price: z.number(),
})

This schema describes one book.

The schema above is created using Zod. It is not a TypeScript type by itself.

If the API sends an array of books, we need an array schema:

const BooksSchema = z.array(BookSchema)

docs.title: Convert the Schema into a TypeScript Type
docs.text:
type Book = z.infer<typeof BookSchema>

Now TypeScript can derive the Book type from the Zod schema.

docs.title: 44. Validate API Data with safeParse
docs.text:
Now the API request:

const btn = document.getElementById("btn") as HTMLButtonElement

// const heading = document.getElementById("heading") as HTMLHeadingElement

let data = []

btn.addEventListener("click", async () => {
    const response = await fetch(
        "https://tsapidemo.lwhh.org/api/v1/books"
    )

    // Use another version to test validation:
    // const response = await fetch(
    //     "https://tsapidemo.lwhh.org/api/v2/books"
    // )

    const books = await response.json()

    const result = BooksSchema.safeParse(books)

    if (!result.success) {
        console.error(result.error.issues)
        return
    }

    console.log(books)

    data = books

    printBookDetails(books[1])
})

This line performs the validation:

const result = BooksSchema.safeParse(books)

If the data is valid:

result.success

will be true.

If the data is invalid, we can inspect:

result.error.issues

and stop processing the invalid data.

docs.title: 45. Create Other Projects with Vite
docs.text:
To create a new Vite project:

npm create vite@latest projectName

Vite can ask us to select a framework, such as:

  • Vanilla
  • React
  • Vue
  • and many others

Then we can select a variant/type, such as:

  • TypeScript
  • JavaScript
  • and others

After that:

npm install

Then:

npm run dev

docs.title: 46. Important tsconfig.json Notes
docs.text:
So far, we manually created tsconfig.json files and used only a small number of options.

But if we look at a tsconfig.json file in a real project or on YouTube, we may see many more settings.

We can automatically create a TypeScript configuration file instead of creating it manually.

Run:

tsc --init

This automatically creates a tsconfig.json with default values and comments.

The generated file also contains documentation links that can be studied for deeper knowledge.

As a beginner, we can make the debugging-related output/source-map options disabled if we do not need them.

docs.title: moduleDetection
docs.text:
By default, we may see:

"moduleDetection": "force"

We can change it to:

"moduleDetection": "auto"

With auto, TypeScript can decide whether a file is a module based on its contents and configuration.

With force, files are treated as modules.

This changes how the generated JavaScript is structured.

docs.title: 47. How Exactly AI Can Help Us
docs.text:
AI can help with tasks such as:

  • Converting an existing project to TypeScript
  • Starting a new project from scratch

Let's see how we can use AI to convert a project into a TypeScript structure.

docs.title: 48. Using AI to Convert an Existing Project to TypeScript
docs.text:
Suppose we have one HTML file containing:

  • HTML
  • CSS
  • JavaScript

Now we want to convert it into a proper TypeScript project structure.

We can use an AI coding tool such as Kilo Code.

Install the Kilo Code extension.

The class also mentions using free models, such as Tencent Hunyuan, depending on what is available in the tool.

docs.title: Create Two Instruction Files
docs.text:
Create:

instruction.md

docs.title: instruction.md
docs.text:
This file contains global instructions.

- Do not use Vite or any bundler.

- Use strict TypeScript.

docs.title: 1. Literal Types
docs.text:
Earlier, when we saw Enum, we used it to restrict values to a fixed set.

We can achieve a similar result using literal types.

The enum version would be conceptually like:

// enum Colors {
//     "Red" = "red",
//     "Green" = "green",
//     "Blue" = "blue"
// }

With literal types:

type Colors = "red" | "green" | "blue"

const c: Colors = "red"

This is useful in very common code.

For example:

type Methods = "GET" | "POST" | "DELETE"

const m: Methods = "PUT"

The last line will show an error because "PUT" is not one of the allowed values.

docs.title: Install TypeScript
docs.text:
npm install -g typescript
tsc --version

tsc = TypeScript Compiler.

docs.title: Needed VS Code Extension
docs.text: • Code Runner

docs.title: File Format
docs.text:
Example:

example.ts

docs.title: 2. Why TypeScript?
3. Run a TypeScript File
docs.text:
We can run a TypeScript file in the terminal using:

node example.ts

or:

bun example.ts

or:

deno example.ts

docs.title: 4. TypeScript → JavaScript Transpilation
docs.text:
Suppose example.ts contains:

function add(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a + b;
}

function subtract(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a - b;
}

function multiply(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a * b;
}

function divide(a: number, b: number): number {
    if (b === 0) {
        throw new Error("Cannot divide by zero");
    }

    return a / b;
}

console.log("add(2, 3) =", add(2, 3));
console.log("subtract(5, 2) =", subtract(5, 2));
console.log("multiply(4, 3) =", multiply(4, 3));
console.log("divide(10, 2) =", divide(10, 2));

Now we want to connect it with an HTML file, so we make an index.html file.

In index.html

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Document</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Demo</h1>
    <script src="example.ts"></script>
</body>
</html>

If we run this file in a browser, we cannot see the expected output in the console because the browser does not execute .ts files like normal JavaScript files. .ts can also be associated with HLS video-stream files, which can make the browser treat the extension differently.

So we have to convert the TypeScript code into JavaScript. This process is called transpiling.

Create a tsconfig.json file:

{
    "compilerOptions": {
        "target": "esnext"
    }
}

Now the compilation part,

In the terminal:

tsc

Run this after each time the TypeScript file is changed.

Or:

tsc --watch

We have to run tsc --watch once, and it will automatically update when the TypeScript file changes. Basically, it stays in watch mode.

After this, a new file will automatically be generated:

example.js

So now we have to change the script location in the HTML file too.

Now modify the script tag in index.html

<body>
    <h1>Demo</h1>
    <script src="example.js"></script>
</body>

Previously it had example.ts; now we changed it to the JavaScript file.

docs.title: 5. Transpile Multiple TypeScript Files into Different Folders
docs.text:
What if we want to transpile multiple .ts files and put the generated JavaScript files into a different folder?

For example:

assets/
├── js/
└── ts/
    ├── ex1.ts
    ├── ex2.ts
    └── ex3.ts

For this, change tsconfig.json:

{
    "compilerOptions": {
        "target": "esnext",
        "outDir": "assets/js",
        "rootDir": "assets/ts"
    }
}

Now in the terminal:

tsc

or:

tsc --watch

After that, the TypeScript files will automatically be transpiled into the js folder.

We mainly need to set:

  • rootDir → where our TypeScript source files are
  • outDir → where the generated JavaScript files should go

docs.title: 6. Handling Errors in TypeScript
docs.text:
Even if there is an error in the TypeScript file, running tsc can still create the JavaScript file. A warning will be shown in the terminal, but this may not be what we want.

If we want TypeScript errors to prevent JavaScript output, we can configure it,

In tsconfig.json

{
    "compilerOptions": {
        "target": "esnext",
        "noEmitOnError": true
    }
}

noEmitOnError: true means TypeScript will not generate the JavaScript output when there are TypeScript errors.

docs.title: 7. Variable Naming Conventions
docs.text:
In TypeScript we can not use variable names such as:

  • name
  • status
  • statusbar
  • toolbar
  • etc.

Check naming conventions separately for better knowledge.

If we want to use those names, we can also do this:

{
    "compilerOptions": {
        "target": "esnext",
        "noEmitOnError": true,
        "moduleDetection": "force"
    }
}

With moduleDetection: "force", TypeScript treats the file as a module.

This can prevent names such as name or status from causing global-scope conflicts.

For better practice, always follow good naming conventions.

docs.title: 1. OOP in TypeScript
docs.text:
Before the OOP example, it is important to understand:

  • public
  • private
  • protected

docs.title: 2. public
docs.text:
A public member can be accessed from:

  • inside the class
  • subclasses
  • outside the class

It is the normal accessible member.

Example:

class Account {
    public name: string

    constructor(name: string) {
        this.name = name
    }
}

const account = new Account("Tanim")

console.log(account.name)

docs.title: 3. private
docs.text:
A private member can be accessed only inside the class where it is declared.

It cannot be accessed directly:

  • from outside the class
  • from a subclass

Example:

class Account {
    private balance: number

    constructor(balance: number) {
        this.balance = balance
    }
}

This is not allowed:

const account = new Account(1000)

console.log(account.balance)

docs.title: 4. protected
docs.text:
A protected member can be accessed:

  • inside the class
  • inside subclasses

But it cannot be accessed directly from outside the class.

Example:

class Account {
    protected balance: number

    constructor(balance: number) {
        this.balance = balance
    }
}

class StudentAccount extends Account {
    showBalance() {
        console.log(this.balance)
    }
}

The subclass can use this.balance, but code outside the class hierarchy cannot directly access it.

docs.title: Quick comparison
docs.text: Modifier Inside class Subclass Outside public ✅ ✅ ✅ protected ✅ ✅ ❌ private ✅ ❌ ❌

docs.title: 6. account.ts
docs.text:
class Account {
    readonly id: number;
    public name: string;
    protected balance: number;

    constructor(id: number, name: string, balance: number) {
        this.id = id;
        this.name = name;
        this.balance = balance;
    }
}

Here:

  • readonly id cannot be reassigned after initialization.
  • public name can be accessed from outside.
  • protected balance can be accessed by the class and its subclasses.

docs.title: 7. Constructor Parameter Properties
docs.text:
We can make the class shorter using parameter properties:

class Account {
    constructor(
        public readonly id: number,
        public name: string,
        protected balance: number
    ) {}
}

TypeScript automatically creates and assigns those properties.

docs.title: 8. Add Methods to the Account Class
docs.text:
class Account {
    constructor(
        public readonly id: number,
        public name: string,
        protected balance: number
    ) {}

    deposit(amount: number): void {
        this.balance += amount
    }

    withdraw(amount: number): void {
        if (this.balance < amount) {
            throw new Error("insufficient balance")
        }

        this.balance -= amount
    }

    status(): void {
        console.log(
            `Account ${this.id} (${this.name}) has a balance of ${this.balance}`
        )
    }
}

docs.title: 9. Interface for Different Account Types
docs.text:
An account can have multiple types, and different account types can have different withdrawal limits.

So we can create an interface above the classes.

interface BaseAccount {
    readonly id: number;
    name: string;

    deposit(amount: number): void;
    withdraw(amount: number): void;
    status(): void;
}

docs.title: Important note about access modifiers in interfaces
docs.text:
We do not use public, private, or protected inside an interface.

Interfaces describe the public shape of an object.

Also, balance is not included in this interface because our balance property is protected.

// balance: number

We cannot describe a protected member as a public interface property.

docs.title: 10. Implement the Interface
docs.text:
class Account implements BaseAccount {
    protected isLimited: boolean = false
    protected limit: number = 0

    constructor(
        public readonly id: number,
        public name: string,
        protected balance: number
    ) {}

    deposit(amount: number): void {
        this.balance += amount
    }

    withdraw(amount: number): void {
        if (this.isLimited && amount > this.limit) {
            throw new Error(
                `You cannot withdraw more than ${this.limit}`
            )
        }

        if (this.balance < amount) {
            throw new Error("insufficient balance")
        }

        this.balance -= amount
    }

    status(): void {
        console.log(
            `Account ${this.id} (${this.name}) has a balance of ${this.balance}`
        )
    }
}

docs.title: 11. Inheritance
docs.text:
Now create specialized account classes.

class StudentAccount extends Account {
    protected isLimited: boolean = true
    protected limit: number = 10000
}

Savings account:

class SavingsAccount extends Account {
    protected isLimited: boolean = true
    protected limit: number = 50000
}

Current account:

class CurrentAccount extends Account {}

docs.title: 12. Use the Student Account
docs.text:
const studentAccount = new StudentAccount(
    153,
    "Student A",
    25000
)

studentAccount.withdraw(5000)
studentAccount.status()

studentAccount.withdraw(15000)
studentAccount.status()

The student account has a withdrawal limit of 10000.

So:

studentAccount.withdraw(5000)

is allowed, while:

studentAccount.withdraw(15000)

will throw an error because it exceeds the limit.

docs.title: TypeScript Functions
docs.text: Functions let us group a set of instructions and run them whenever we need them.

docs.title: 1. Writing a Function
docs.text:
The basic syntax of a TypeScript function is:

function functionName(parameter: type): returnType {
    // function body
    return value
}

For example:

function greet(name: string): string {
    return `Hello, ${name}`
}

const message = greet("Tanim")

console.log(message)

Here:

  • name: string means the function accepts a string parameter.
  • : string after the closing parenthesis is the return type.
  • return sends a value back to the place where the function was called.

docs.title: 2. Function Parameters
docs.text:
We should specify the type of every parameter.

function add(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a + b
}

console.log(add(5, 3))

The function accepts two numbers and returns a number.

If we pass a string instead of a number, TypeScript will show an error:

add("5", 3)

docs.title: 3. Return Type
docs.text:
The return type tells TypeScript what kind of value the function will return.

function multiply(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a * b
}

If a function returns a string, its return type should be string:

function getFullName(firstName: string, lastName: string): string {
    return `${firstName} ${lastName}`
}

docs.title: 4. A Function Without a Return Value
docs.text:
If a function does not return a value, we can use the void return type.

function showMessage(message: string): void {
    console.log(message)
}

showMessage("TypeScript is useful")

The function performs an action, but it does not return a value.

docs.title: 5. Optional Parameters
docs.text:
We can make a parameter optional by adding ? after its name.

function greetUser(name: string, title?: string): string {
    if (title) {
        return `Hello, ${title} ${name}`
    }

    return `Hello, ${name}`
}

console.log(greetUser("Tanim"))
console.log(greetUser("Tanim", "Mr."))

An optional parameter must come after the required parameters.

docs.title: 6. Default Parameters
docs.text:
Instead of making a parameter optional, we can give it a default value.

function welcome(name: string, greeting: string = "Hello"): string {
    return `${greeting}, ${name}`
}

console.log(welcome("Tanim"))
console.log(welcome("Tanim", "Good morning"))

If the caller does not provide greeting, TypeScript uses the default value.

docs.title: 7. Arrow Functions
docs.text:
We can also write a function using arrow-function syntax.

const subtract = (a: number, b: number): number => {
    return a - b
}

console.log(subtract(10, 4))

For a one-line function, we can write it more shortly:

const square = (number: number): number => number * number

console.log(square(5))

docs.title: 8. Function Expressions
docs.text:
A function can be stored in a variable.

const divide = function (a: number, b: number): number {
    return a / b
}

console.log(divide(10, 2))

The parameter types and return type are written in the same way as a normal function.

docs.title: 9. Callback Functions
docs.text:
A callback is a function passed as an argument to another function.

function processNumber(
    number: number,
    callback: (value: number) => number
): number {
    return callback(number)
}

const result = processNumber(5, (value: number): number => value * 2)

console.log(result)

Here, (value: number) => number describes a function that accepts a number and returns a number.

docs.title: 10. Rest Parameters
docs.text:
Rest parameters allow a function to accept any number of arguments of the same type.

function sum(...numbers: number[]): number {
    return numbers.reduce((total, number) => total + number, 0)
}

console.log(sum(1, 2, 3))
console.log(sum(10, 20, 30, 40))

The ...numbers parameter collects all the provided numbers into an array.

docs.title: 11. Function Returning a Tuple
docs.text:
A function can return a tuple when it returns multiple fixed-position values.

type Division = [number, number]

function divideWithRemainder(a: number, b: number): Division {
    const quotient = Math.floor(a / b)
    const remainder = a % b

    return [quotient, remainder]
}

const result: Division = divideWithRemainder(7, 2)

console.log(result)

The return value is a tuple containing the quotient and the remainder.

docs.title: 1. Generic
docs.text:
Generic is a powerful TypeScript feature that lets us work with a dynamic type.

Suppose we have:

const fruits: string[] = [
    "apple",
    "banana",
    "cherry",
    "date",
    "elderberry"
]

const numbers: number[] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

If we write:

function getFirstItem(items: string[]): string {
    return items[0]
}

The function is fixed to string.

It accepts strings and returns a string.

If we change it to number, then it would work only with numbers.

But we want a way where the return type is dynamic.

In other words, if we pass strings, we want a string back. If we pass numbers, we want a number back.

docs.title: Generic solution
docs.text:
const fruits: string[] = [
    "apple",
    "banana",
    "cherry",
    "date",
    "elderberry"
]

const numbers: number[] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

function getFirstItem<T>(items: T[]): T {
    return items[0]
}

const firstFruit = getFirstItem(fruits)
const firstNumber = getFirstItem(numbers)

console.log(firstFruit.toUpperCase())
console.log(firstNumber.toFixed(2))

Here we do not use a fixed data type.

T represents the type that is passed to the function.

The <T> portion identifies the generic type, and TypeScript automatically determines what T should be from the argument.

So:

getFirstItem(fruits)

makes T become string.

And:

getFirstItem(numbers)

makes T become number.

docs.title: 2. Generic with API Fetching
docs.text:
Let's see how we can use generics with APIs.

First, define our types:

type User = {
    id: number
    name: string
    email: string
}

type Product = {
    id: number
    name: string
    price: number
}

type Order = {
    id: number
    userId: number
    total: number,
    date: string,
    status: "pending" | "shipped" | "delivered"
}

Example API endpoints:

/api/users
/api/products
/api/orders
Normal TypeScript approachBetter: Generic API function 
async function getUsers(): Promise<User[]> {
    const data = await fetch("/api/users")
    return data.json()
}

async function getProducts(): Promise<Product[]> {
    const data = await fetch("/api/products")
    return data.json()
}

async function getOrders(): Promise<Order[]> {
    const data = await fetch("/api/orders")
    return data.json()
}

const users = await getUsers()
const products = await getProducts()
const orders = await getOrders()

Here we need three different functions for three different types of API data.

We can make the code simpler and shorter using a generic.

async function get<T>(apiEndpoint: string): Promise<T> {
    const data = await fetch(apiEndpoint)
    return data.json()
}

const users = await get<User[]>("/api/users")
const products = await get<Product[]>("/api/products")
const orders = await get<Order[]>("/api/orders")

This single function works for both a single value and an array, depending on the generic type we provide.

Important: Read more about generics because they are very important in TypeScript.

docs.title: 1. Script Bundle
docs.text:
In real projects, the entire project script is usually not written in one TypeScript file.

Different responsibilities are separated into different .ts files.

Then we can bundle those TypeScript files and create one JavaScript output file.

This is a more advanced process.

Let's use the same task-management project to learn bundling.

docs.title: 2. Create a src Folder
docs.text:
Inside src, create two files.

src/
├── seed.ts
└── script.ts

docs.title: 3. src/seed.ts
docs.text:
export type Task = {
    id: number;
    title: string;
    completed: boolean;
}

export let tasks: Task[] = []

export let nextId = 1

We could change exported variables directly, but directly changing shared state is generally not the best practice.

So we can use a function:

export function getNextId(): number {
    return nextId++
}

Now the ID is changed through a function instead of directly modifying the variable.

docs.title: Sample task function
docs.text:
export function createSampleTasks(): void {
    const samples: Omit<Task, "id">[] = [
        { title: "Buy groceries", completed: true },
        { title: "Finish TypeScript homework", completed: false },
        { title: "Call the dentist", completed: false },
        { title: "Water the plants", completed: true },
        { title: "Refuel the scooter", completed: false },
    ]

    samples.forEach((sample) => {
        tasks.push({
            id: nextId++,
            title: sample.title,
            completed: sample.completed
        })
    })
}

docs.title: Why are we using export now?
docs.text:
In the earlier version, everything was inside one file, so we did not need to export anything.

Now the code is split into multiple files.

Modern TypeScript projects commonly organize code into modules.

So we export the things that another file needs to import.

docs.title: 4. Import from seed.ts
docs.text: Because we moved some code from script.ts into seed.ts, we need to import those things into script.ts.

docs.title: 5. src/script.ts
docs.text:
import {
    tasks,
    getNextId,
    createSampleTasks
} from "./seed"

const form = document.getElementById("task-form") as HTMLFormElement
const input = document.getElementById("task-input") as HTMLInputElement
const list = document.getElementById("task-list") as HTMLUListElement
const exportButton = document.getElementById("export") as HTMLButtonElement

Then:

function renderTasks(): void {
    list.innerHTML = ""

    tasks.forEach((task) => {
        const li = document.createElement("li")

        const checkbox = document.createElement("input")
        checkbox.type = "checkbox"
        checkbox.checked = task.completed

        checkbox.addEventListener("change", () => {
            task.completed = checkbox.checked
        })

        const span = document.createElement("span")
        span.textContent = task.title

        li.append(checkbox, span)
        list.append(li)
    })
}

Add task:

function addTask(title: string): void {
    tasks.push({
        id: getNextId(),
        title: title,
        completed: false
    })

    renderTasks()
}

Form handling:

form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
    event.preventDefault()

    addTask(input.value)

    input.value = ""
    input.focus()
})

docs.title: 6. TypeScript Modules with Node.js
docs.text:
Let's make the example a module.

Create mathlib.ts:

export function add(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a + b
}

export function subtract(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a - b
}

We can also export at the bottom:

function add(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a + b
}

function subtract(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a - b
}

export { add, subtract }

Then in example.ts:

import { add, subtract } from "./mathlib.ts"

console.log(add(10, 6))
console.log(subtract(22, 6))

The behavior can differ depending on the runtime and its TypeScript/module support.

In the original class example:

node example.ts

was shown as producing an error for this module setup, while:

bun example.ts

and:

deno example.ts

were shown as working.

docs.title: 7. Fixing Node's Module Setup
docs.text:
To fix the module setup for Node, create:

package.json

with:

{
    "type": "module"
}

After this, the module configuration is explicitly set to ES modules.

docs.title: 1. Objects
docs.text: Let's go to objects.

docs.title: 2. Using type
docs.text:
type User = {
    id: number,
    name: string
}

const person: User = {
    id: 16,
    name: "hasin"
}

const person2: User = {
    id: 18,
    name: "jane"
}

docs.title: 3. Using interface
docs.text:
We can use an interface too. It works similarly to type for this kind of object definition.

With an interface, we do not use the = sign.

interface User {
    id: number,
    name: string
}

const person: User = {
    id: 16,
    name: "hasin"
}

const person2: User = {
    id: 18,
    name: "jane"
}

docs.title: 4. A More Complex Interface Example
docs.text:
interface AppConfig {
    appName: string;
    version: string; // "1.6.0"
    debug: boolean;
    port: number;

    database: {
        host: string;
        port: number;
        username: string;
        password: string;
    };

    features: {
        registration: boolean;
        darkMode: boolean;
    };
}

const config: AppConfig = {}

Here, database and features are nested objects.

We can also create separate interfaces for them. That can make the code cleaner and easier to understand.

interface Database {
    host: string;
    port: number;
    username: string;
    password: string;
}

interface AppConfig {
    appName: string;
    version: string; // "1.6.0"
    debug: boolean;
    port: number;
    database: Database;

    features: {
        registration: boolean;
        darkMode: boolean;
    };
}

In the interface above, we could also use a type instead of an interface.

docs.title: Semicolon vs comma
docs.text:
Here we use ;:

interface Database {
    host: string;
    port: number;
}

We could also use commas. Both are valid, but semicolons are preferable in this style.

docs.title: type vs interface
docs.text: For many object-shape definitions, we can use either type or interface.

docs.title: 1. TypeScript with HTML
docs.text:
Suppose an HTML file has:

  • one input with id="email"
  • one button with id="send"
Normal approachBetter: Generic querySelector 
const input = document.getElementById("email") as HTMLInputElement
const button = document.getElementById("send") as HTMLButtonElement

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
    console.log(`Subscription complete for ${input.value}`)
})

HTMLInputElement is added because TypeScript knows that getElementById() can return null, and it does not automatically know that the returned element is specifically an input element.

In JavaScript, we do not have to write HTMLInputElement or HTMLButtonElement.

We can do the same thing using a generic:

const input = document.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>("#email")
const button = document.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>("#send")

if (button && input) {
    button.addEventListener("click", () => {
        console.log(`Subscription complete for ${input.value}`)
    })
}

The generic version is better because:

  1. We can specify the element type.
  2. We can also perform a null check.
  3. TypeScript can understand the element type.

So the generic version is generally much better.

docs.title: 2. Project: Task Management Application
docs.text:
Let's build a small task manager application.

Suppose we already have an HTML file.

docs.title: 3. script.ts
docs.text:
First, define the task type:

type Task = {
    id: number;
    title: string;
    completed: boolean;
}

Get the HTML elements:

const form = document.getElementById("task-form") as HTMLFormElement
const input = document.getElementById("task-input") as HTMLInputElement
const list = document.getElementById("task-list") as HTMLUListElement

Create the task storage:

let tasks: Task[] = []
let nextId = 1

docs.title: 4. Create Sample Tasks
docs.text:
Let's create a function for adding sample tasks.

function createSampleTasks(): void {
    const samples: Omit<Task, "id">[] = [
        { title: "Buy groceries", completed: true },
        { title: "Finish TypeScript homework", completed: false },
        { title: "Call the dentist", completed: false },
        { title: "Water the plants", completed: true },
    ]

    samples.forEach((sample) => {
        tasks.push({
            id: nextId++,
            title: sample.title,
            completed: sample.completed
        })
    })
}

createSampleTasks()

console.log(tasks)

Omit<Task, "id"> means all the properties of Task except id.

The id is generated automatically.

docs.title: 5. HTML Task List
docs.text:
In index.html:

<section>
    <h2>Tasks</h2>
    <ul id="task-list">
        <!-- All rendered task data will appear here -->
    </ul>
</section>

docs.title: 6. Render Tasks
docs.text:
Now we need to render the tasks into the HTML file.

Add this after the previous code in script.ts:

function renderTasks(): void {
    list.innerHTML = ""

    tasks.forEach((task) => {
        const li = document.createElement("li")

        const checkbox = document.createElement("input")
        checkbox.type = "checkbox"
        checkbox.checked = task.completed

        checkbox.addEventListener("change", () => {
            task.completed = checkbox.checked
        })

        const span = document.createElement("span")
        span.textContent = task.title

        li.append(checkbox, span)
        list.append(li)
    })
}

docs.title: 7. Add a New Task
docs.text:
Now let's add a function for adding a new task.

function addTask(title: string): void {
    tasks.push({
        id: nextId++,
        title: title,
        completed: false
    })

    renderTasks()
}

Then handle the form submission:

form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
    event.preventDefault()

    addTask(input.value)

    input.value = ""
    input.focus()
})

docs.title: What does event.preventDefault() do?
docs.text:
When a form is submitted, the browser has a default behavior. Usually, the browser may submit the form and reload/navigate the page.

event.preventDefault()

stops that default browser behavior.

This allows our TypeScript code to handle the form submission ourselves without the page being reloaded.

docs.title: What does input.focus() do?
docs.text:
input.focus()

puts the keyboard focus back into the input field.

For example:

  1. Type a task name.
  2. Press Enter.
  3. The task is added.
  4. The input is cleared.
  5. input.focus() puts the cursor back into the input.
  6. We can immediately type the next task without clicking the input again.

docs.title: 8. Fetch API Data with a Button
docs.text:
Suppose we have a button with the ID btn.

const btn = document.getElementById("btn") as HTMLButtonElement

// const heading = document.getElementById("heading") as HTMLHeadingElement

let data = []

btn.addEventListener("click", async () => {
    const response = await fetch(
        "https://tsapidemo.lwhh.org/api/v1/books"
    )

    const books = await response.json()

    console.log(books)

    data = books

    printBookDetails(books[1])
})

Function:

function printBookDetails(book) {
    // console.clear();

    console.log("ID:", book.id)
    console.log("Title:", book.title)
    console.log("Author:", book.author)
    console.log("Category:", book.category)
    console.log("Price:", book.price)
}

docs.title: What did we do?
docs.text:
First, we fetched data from the API URL.

Then we converted the response into JSON and stored it in books.

Then:

printBookDetails(books[1])

passes one book to the function, so we can see that book's information.

docs.title: 9. Why Validate API Data?
docs.text:
There is a problem.

What if, in the future, someone adds a book with a different key-value structure?

What if there are multiple categories?

What if another key is added?

Our code assumes that the API response always has the exact structure we expect.

So whenever we use API data, we should validate the data to make sure it has the format we expect.

For data validation, we can use a library called Zod.

docs.title: Install Zod
docs.text:
In the terminal:

npm install zod

After installing it, import Zod:

import { z } from "zod"

Importing Zod alone is not enough.

We also need to create a schema describing the format we expect from the API.

docs.title: 11. Book Schema
docs.text:
const BookSchema = z.object({
    id: z.number(),
    title: z.string(),
    author: z.string(),
    category: z.string(),
    price: z.number(),
})

This schema describes one book.

The schema above is created using Zod. It is not a TypeScript type by itself.

If the API sends an array of books, we need an array schema:

const BooksSchema = z.array(BookSchema)

docs.title: 12. Convert the Schema into a TypeScript Type
docs.text:
type Book = z.infer<typeof BookSchema>

Now TypeScript can derive the Book type from the Zod schema.

docs.title: 13. Validate API Data with safeParse
docs.text:
Now the API request:

const btn = document.getElementById("btn") as HTMLButtonElement

// const heading = document.getElementById("heading") as HTMLHeadingElement

let data = []

btn.addEventListener("click", async () => {
    const response = await fetch(
        "https://tsapidemo.lwhh.org/api/v1/books"
    )

    // Use another version to test validation:
    // const response = await fetch(
    //     "https://tsapidemo.lwhh.org/api/v2/books"
    // )

    const books = await response.json()

    const result = BooksSchema.safeParse(books)

    if (!result.success) {
        console.error(result.error.issues)
        return
    }

    console.log(books)

    data = books

    printBookDetails(books[1])
})

This line performs the validation:

const result = BooksSchema.safeParse(books)

If the data is valid:

result.success

will be true.

If the data is invalid, we can inspect:

result.error.issues

and stop processing the invalid data.

docs.title: 14. Create Other Projects with Vite

To create a new Vite project:

npm create vite@latest projectName
