docs.title: 15. How Exactly AI Can Help Us
docs.text:
AI can help with tasks such as:

  • Converting an existing project to TypeScript
  • Starting a new project from scratch

Let's see how we can use AI to convert a project into a TypeScript structure.

docs.title: 16. Using AI to Convert an Existing Project to TypeScript
docs.text:
Suppose we have one HTML file containing:

  • HTML
  • CSS
  • JavaScript

Now we want to convert it into a proper TypeScript project structure.

We can use an AI coding tool such as Kilo Code.

Install the Kilo Code extension.

The class also mentions using free models, such as Tencent Hunyuan, depending on what is available in the tool.

docs.title: 17. Create Two Instruction Files
docs.text:
Create:

instruction.md
task.md

docs.title: instruction.md
docs.text:
This file contains global instructions.

# Instructions

- Keep the code simple and beginner-friendly.
- Use plain TypeScript with `tsc`.
- Do not use Vite or any bundler.
- Never use `any`.
- Use strict TypeScript.
- Use modern ES modules.
- Keep the original functionality unchanged.

The benefit is that we do not have to repeat the same instructions in every prompt.

We can tell the AI to follow the instructions in this file.

docs.title: task.md
docs.text:
This file contains the specific task.

# Task

Convert the provided HTML file into a working TypeScript project.

- Move CSS to `assets/css/style.css`.
- Move JavaScript to `assets/ts/main.ts`.
- Replace JavaScript with TypeScript.
- Fetch data from the API endpoint.
- Update the HTML to load `assets/css/style.css` and `assets/js/main.js`.
- Create a minimal `tsconfig.json` that compiles `assets/ts` to `assets/js`.
- Load live books data from https://tsapidemo.lwhh.org/api/v1/books

docs.title: 18. Using Kilo Code
docs.text:
The class workflow is:

  1. Install Kilo Code from the extension/library.
  2. Open the command palette.
  3. Select the Kilo Code toggle command.

The class also mentions:

Ctrl + Alt + B

as a shortcut.

Then open the Kilo Code chat window.

Use a prompt like:

Implement this task @task.md - follow the instructions @instruction.md

Files such as:

@task.md
@instruction.md

can be attached/referenced in the chat.

The class notes mention that files can be dragged into the chat box, and pressing Shift while dragging can be used to drop/reference them.

Then select the model you want to use.

The class example uses a free Tencent model.

docs.title: 19. Choosing a Mode
docs.text:
Another important setting is the mode.

If the task is small, we can use Code mode.

For a larger task involving things like:

  • calculation
  • deeper thinking
  • exploration
  • complex planning

we can use Plan mode first.

docs.title: 20. Creating a New Project from Scratch with AI
docs.text:
We can also use AI to create a completely new project.

Again, create two files:

instruction.md
task.md

docs.title: 21. instruction.md
docs.text:
# Instructions

- Keep the code simple and beginner-friendly.
- Use plain TypeScript with `tsc`.
- Do not use Vite or any bundler.
- Never use `any`.
- Enable strict mode.
- Use `ESNext` for `target` and `module`.
- Use modern ES modules.
- Create a clean, minimal design with ample whitespace.

docs.title: 22. task.md
docs.text:
# Task

Create a simple Book Catalog application.

Create a clean, minimal `markup.html` with ample whitespace.

Then convert it into a TypeScript project.

- Keep the original markup in `markup.html`.
- Move CSS to `assets/css/style.css`.
- Move TypeScript to `assets/ts/main.ts`.
- Compile TypeScript to `assets/js/main.js`.
- Create a minimal `tsconfig.json` using `ESNext`.
- Load live books data from https://tsapidemo.lwhh.org/api/v1/books.
- Display the books in a clean, responsive catalog.
- Update the page to load the generated CSS and JavaScript.

Then use the same process:

  1. Open Kilo Code.
  2. Use the shortcut if configured.
  3. Open the chat.
  4. Provide:
Implement this task @task.md - follow the instructions @instruction.md
  1. Select the tool/model.
  2. Select the appropriate mode.
  3. Run it.

Here we specifically told the AI to use ESNext, for example.

docs.title: 23. The Main Idea Behind instruction.md and task.md
docs.text: The basic idea is:

docs.title: instruction.md
docs.text:
Keep the global rules here.

Examples:

  • coding style
  • TypeScript rules
  • libraries to avoid
  • whether any is allowed
  • module system
  • design preferences

docs.title: task.md
docs.text:
Keep the specific task here.

Examples:

  • what project to create
  • what files to create
  • where CSS should go
  • where TypeScript should go
  • which API to use
  • what the UI should do

The more specific and clear we can make the instructions, the better the AI can organize the code.

docs.title: 24. AI Tools Mentioned for Design
docs.text:
Some AI tools mentioned for design-related work:

  • Lovable
  • v0
  • Bolt

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Topic Main idea Type annotations Tell TypeScript what type a value should have Arrays string[], number[] Objects type or interface Tuple Fixed order/number of array elements Enum Restrict values to named constants Union Allow multiple possible types Literal type Allow a fixed set of exact values Omit Remove selected properties from a type Optional property property?: type Generic Work with dynamic/reusable types Set Store unique values Map Store key-value pairs public Accessible everywhere protected Class + subclasses private Only the declaring class readonly Prevent reassignment Rollup Bundle modules into a final JavaScript file Tree shaking Remove unused code from the bundle Vite Quickly create and run modern projects Zod Runtime data validation tsconfig.json TypeScript compiler configuration AI instructions Separate global rules from individual tasks

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
The most important ideas from this class are:

  1. TypeScript adds static type information to JavaScript.
  2. tsc can transpile TypeScript into JavaScript.
  3. tsconfig.json controls TypeScript compilation.
  4. type and interface are both useful for describing object shapes.
  5. Tuples describe fixed-position arrays.
  6. Enums and literal types can restrict values.
  7. Union types allow more than one possible type.
  8. Utility types such as Omit help create reusable type definitions.
  9. Optional properties use ?.
  10. Generics make functions reusable while keeping type safety.
  11. Map and Set are useful TypeScript-friendly data structures.
  12. DOM elements can be typed using assertions or generic DOM APIs.
  13. Larger projects should separate code into modules.
  14. Rollup can bundle modules and perform tree shaking.
  15. TypeScript can be used for server-side applications.
  16. public, protected, and private control class member access.
  17. Vite makes project setup and development faster.
  18. Production builds should be tested with npm run build and npm run preview.
  19. API responses should be validated instead of blindly trusting their structure.
  20. Zod can be used to validate API data at runtime.
  21. AI can help convert existing projects or create new projects when given clear instructions.
  22. Keeping global instructions in instruction.md and project-specific work in task.md makes AI-assisted development more organized.

End of notes — TypeScript crash course by LearnwithHasinHayder

docs.title: 1. Rollup Bundler
docs.text:
Now we have two TypeScript files and want to bundle them into one JavaScript file.

We will use Rollup.

We install packages through package.json, because this is the normal way to manage JavaScript project dependencies.

docs.title: 2. package.json
docs.text:
Create a new package.json:

{
    "name": "task-manager",
    "version": "1.0.0",
    "private": true,
    "type": "module",
    "scripts": {
        "build": "rollup -c",
        "watch": "rollup -c -w"
    },
    "devDependencies": {
        "@rollup/plugin-typescript": "^12.1.0",
        "rollup": "^4.24.0",
        "tslib": "^2.8.0",
        "typescript": "^5.9.0"
    }
}

docs.title: 3. .gitignore
docs.text:
Create another file:

.gitignore

Add:

node_modules

docs.title: Why do we add node_modules to .gitignore?
docs.text:
node_modules contains installed dependencies.

We normally do not push this huge generated folder to GitHub.

Instead, we push:

  • package.json
  • package-lock.json (when generated)

Then another developer or the deployment platform can run:

npm install

and recreate node_modules.

docs.title: 4. Install the packages
docs.text:
In the terminal:

npm install

docs.title: 5. rollup.config.js
docs.text:
Create:

rollup.config.js

Add:

import typescript from "@rollup/plugin-typescript";

export default {
    input: "src/script.ts",

    output: {
        file: "dist/app.js",
        format: "iife"
    },

    plugins: [
        typescript()
    ]
};

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
npm run build

or:

rollup -c

The bundled output will be:

dist/app.js

docs.title: 6. Update index.html
docs.text:
Change the script location:

<script src="dist/app.js"></script>

Instead of loading the individual TypeScript file.

docs.title: 7. Watch Mode
docs.text:
To automatically rebuild when files change:

npm run watch

or:

rollup -c -w

docs.title: 8. Rollup Tree Shaking
docs.text:
Tree shaking is an important built-in Rollup feature.

Suppose we have:

function deleteTask() {
    console.log("will implement")
}

But this function is never used.

Rollup can detect that it is unused and remove it from the final bundle.

So unused code does not need to be included in the production bundle.

This process is called tree shaking.

docs.title: 9. Node.js with TypeScript
docs.text:
Server-side applications such as:

  • Node.js
  • Bun
  • Deno

can work with TypeScript.

Example example.ts:

function add(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a + b
}

function subtract(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a - b
}

console.log(add(10, 6))
console.log(subtract(22, 6))

Run:

node example.ts

or:

bun example.ts

or:

deno example.ts

The class notes point out that Node.js has been adding TypeScript support and that modern Node can run TypeScript files directly in supported situations.

docs.title: 10. Creating a Modern TypeScript Project with Vite
docs.text:
Developers do not want to waste time manually creating every folder and configuration file.

They often use Vite to speed up project setup and development.

In the terminal:

npm create vite@latest project_name

Then:

cd project_name
npm install

Open the project in an IDE such as VS Code.

Run:

npm run dev

Vite automatically sets up many things for us.

We can still modify the generated project.

docs.title: 11. Development vs Production
docs.text:
During development, we can use:

npm run dev

to run the development server and visually see the project.

But before deployment, we should make sure the project also works correctly as production code.

So run:

npm run build

Then:

npm run preview

npm run preview lets us visualize the production build.

The preview is based on the build output.

docs.title: Development
docs.text: npm run dev

docs.title: Production build
docs.text: npm run build

docs.title: Preview production build
docs.text: npm run preview

docs.title: 12. GitHub and Deployment
docs.text:
While developing, we normally do not push generated folders such as:

dist/
node_modules/

to GitHub.

So .gitignore should at least contain:

node_modules
dist

We can push the whole source project to GitHub.

Then on a deployment platform:

  1. Log in with GitHub.
  2. Add a new project.
  3. Select the repository.
  4. Deploy.

For example, Vercel can automatically build and deploy the project.

docs.title: 13. Important tsconfig.json Notes
docs.text:
So far, we manually created tsconfig.json files and used only a small number of options.

But if we look at a tsconfig.json file in a real project or on YouTube, we may see many more settings.

We can automatically create a TypeScript configuration file instead of creating it manually.

Run:

tsc --init

This automatically creates a tsconfig.json with default values and comments.

The generated file also contains documentation links that can be studied for deeper knowledge.

As a beginner, we can make the debugging-related output/source-map options disabled if we do not need them.

docs.title: 14. moduleDetection
docs.text:
By default, we may see:

"moduleDetection": "force"

We can change it to:

"moduleDetection": "auto"

With auto, TypeScript can decide whether a file is a module based on its contents and configuration.

With force, files are treated as modules.

This changes how the generated JavaScript is structured.

docs.title: 1. Union Type
docs.text:
A union type lets a value have more than one possible type.

type ID = string | number;

const id: ID = "g-016"

function printId(id: ID) {
    console.log(`ID: ${id}`)
}

printId("g-017")

docs.title: 2. Another Union Example
docs.text:
type Rectangle = {
    height: number;
    width: number;
}

type Circle = {
    radius: number;
}

type Square = {
    length: number;
}

function calculateArea(shape: Rectangle | Circle | Square): number {
    if ("radius" in shape) {
        return Math.PI * shape.radius * shape.radius
    }

    else if ("length" in shape) {
        return shape.length * shape.length
    }

    return shape.height * shape.width
}

We can make the union reusable:

type Shape = Rectangle | Circle | Square

function calculateArea(shape: Shape): number {
    // ...
}

docs.title: 1. Basic Types
docs.text:
const country: string = "Bangladesh"
const n: number = 16

const status: boolean = true

If we write:

let x

it will be undefined.

We can see this by writing:

console.log(typeof x)

docs.title: Array type
docs.text:
const countries: string[] = [
    "bangladesh",
    "india",
    "US",
    "UK"
]

docs.title: 2. Arrays
docs.text:
const stdName: string[] = []

stdName.push("tanim")
stdName.push("manim")
stdName.push("kanim")

Another example:

const marks: number[] = [2, 1]

marks.push(7)

docs.title: 3. Tuple
docs.text:
A tuple lets us describe an array with a fixed number and order of element types.

type Point = [number, number]

const location1: Point = [12, 34]

const dhakaLocation: Point = [23.7330, 90.40]

console.log(dhakaLocation)
console.log(dhakaLocation[0])

Another example:

type Player = [string, string, number]

const players: Player[] = [
    ["ronaldo", "portugal", 7],
    ["messi", "argentina", 10]
]

Another example:

type OrderItem = [number, number]

const item: OrderItem = [7, 16]

item.push(20)

console.log(item)

docs.title: Interesting tuple problem
docs.text:
While defining OrderItem, we said it contains two values:

type OrderItem = [number, number]

But JavaScript arrays are still mutable, so push() can add another value:

item.push(20)

This can be surprising because the tuple was intended to represent exactly two values.

For this kind of situation, we can use readonly.

type OrderItem = readonly [number, number]

const item: OrderItem = [7, 16]

item.push(20)

Now the last line will show an error because we are trying to modify a readonly tuple.

Another Tuple Example

type Division = [number, number]

function divide(a: number, b: number): Division {
    const quotient = Math.floor(a / b)
    const remainder = a % b

    return [quotient, remainder]
}

const result: Division = divide(7, 2)

console.log(result)

docs.title: 4. Enum
docs.text:
Suppose we have a T-shirt product with different sizes and colors.

type TeeShirt = {
    size: number,
    color: string
}

const t1: TeeShirt = {
    size: 42,
    color: "red"
}

const t2: TeeShirt = {
    size: 38,
    color: "yellow"
}

const t3: TeeShirt = {
    size: 40,
    color: "green"
}

What if the product never had a yellow color, or yellow is currently unavailable? But, we still accidentally wrote yellow in the code.

If we want to prevent this, we can use an enum. 

enum TColors {
    Red = "red",
    Green = "green",
}

type TeeShirt = {
    size: number,
    color: TColors
}

const t1: TeeShirt = {
    size: 42,
    color: TColors.Red
}

const t2: TeeShirt = {
    size: 38,
    color: "yellow"
}

The yellow line will show an error.

And here, we have to use TColors. and then select one of the available colors.

const t3: TeeShirt = {
    size: 40,
    color: TColors.Green
}

docs.title: Another Way to Use Enum
docs.text:
enum Status {
    draft,
    private,
    public
}

Previously, we explicitly assigned values such as:

Red = "red"

Here we did not use =.

In this situation, TypeScript automatically assigns numeric values:

draft   → 0
private → 1
public  → 2

Then:

type Article = {
    id: number;
    title: string;
    status: Status;
};

const article1: Article = {
    id: 1,
    title: "Understanding TypeScript Enums",
    status: Status.draft
};

const article2: Article = {
    id: 2,
    title: "Advanced TypeScript Types",
    status: Status.public
};

console.log(article2)

The status value in the output will be 2.

That 2 is not the article's id. It is the numeric enum value for Status.public.

docs.title: 6. Map & Set
docs.text:
Set and Map are useful for storing:

  • unique values → Set
  • key-value pairs → Map

docs.title: 7. Set
docs.text:
Normal JavaScriptTypeScript 
const data = new Set()

data.add("abc")
data.add(30)
data.add(true)

All these data types can be added in a normal JavaScript Set.

We can make the type fixed:

const data = new Set<string>()

Now only string values can be added.

docs.title: 8. Map
docs.text:
Normal JavaScriptTypeScript 
const players = new Map()

players.set("Ronaldo", 7)
players.set(10, "Messi")
players.set("Neymar", "brazil")

const players = new Map<string, number>()

players.set("Ronaldo", 7)
players.set("Messy", 10)

One important thing here is:

Map<keyType, valueType>

The first type is the key, and the second type is the value.

Map keys are unique.

If we use the same key again, the new value replaces the old value.

For example:

players.set("messy", 13)
players.set("messy", 10)

The second line rewrites the value associated with "messy".

So the final value for "messy" is 10.

Because a Map rewrites the value for an existing key, we can use it as a simple counting storage.

docs.title: 9. Practical Map Example: Juice Shop
docs.text:
Suppose we have a juice shop.

We want to automatically count how many times each juice has been ordered.

const orders = new Map<string, number>()

function addOrder(juice: string, count: number) {
    const quantity = orders.get(juice) || 0
    orders.set(juice, quantity + count)
}

addOrder("mango", 2)
addOrder("mango", 4)
addOrder("apple", 5)
addOrder("banana", 1)
addOrder("apple", 2)

console.log(orders)

The Map keeps the total quantity for each juice.

docs.title: 1. Omit Type
docs.text:
TypeScript has many built-in utility types.

Let's first see how we would solve a problem normally.

type User = {
    id: number
    name: string
    email: string
}

const users: User[] = []

let lastId: number = 0

function addUser(name: string, email: string): User {
    const user: User = {
        id: ++lastId,
        name,
        email,
    }

    users.push(user)
    return user
}

Here, we want to pass only name and email. We do not want to pass id, because id should be generated automatically.

addUser("Alice", "alice@example.com")
addUser("Bob", "bob@example.com")

console.log(users)

We can solve this using TypeScript's built-in Omit utility type.

type User = {
    id: number
    name: string
    email: string
}

const users: User[] = []

let lastId: number = 0

function addUser(user: Omit<User, "id">): User {
    const newUser: User = {
        ...user,
        id: ++lastId
    }

    users.push(newUser)
    return newUser
}

Omit<User, "id"> accepts all the properties of User except id.

The ...user part is JavaScript's built-in spread operator.

Because user is an object, we pass the properties as key-value pairs:

addUser({
    name: "Alice",
    email: "alice@example.com"
})

addUser({
    name: "Bob",
    email: "bob@example.com"
})

console.log(users)

docs.title: 2. Optional Properties
docs.text:
We can solve the same problem in another way by making the id property optional.

type User = {
    id?: number
    name: string
    email: string
}

const users: User[] = []

let lastId: number = 0

function addUser(user: User): User {
    const newUser: User = {
        id: ++lastId,
        ...user
    }

    users.push(newUser)
    return newUser
}

addUser({
    name: "Alice",
    email: "alice@example.com"
})

addUser({
    name: "Bob",
    email: "bob@example.com"
})

console.log(users)

Adding ? after a property name makes it an optional property.

That means the property can be provided, but it does not have to be provided.

TypeScript has many other interesting built-in utility types. Study them for better knowledge.

docs.title: Pi Camera Setup on Ubuntu 22.04 LTS
docs.text:
Context

This guide covers the full dependency maze for the OV5647 (Rev 1.3) sensor on a Raspberry Pi 4 running Ubuntu 22.04 LTS — including the Meson version fix, building libcamera from source, and all usage commands.

docs.title: Physical Check First
docs.text:
Before touching any software:

Hardware Checklist

  • Ribbon cable must be in the CSI (Camera) port — between the HDMI and Audio jack, NOT the DSI (Display) port
  • Silver pins on the ribbon cable must face the HDMI ports
  • Check your sensor model on the green PCB — if it says Rev 1.3, the dtoverlay=ov5647 line below is mandatory

docs.title: Phase 1: Firmware Configuration
docs.text:
The Pi 4 won't auto-detect the OV5647 Rev 1.3 sensor. You have to tell it manually.

sudo nano /boot/firmware/config.txt

Scroll to the bottom and make these two changes:

Step 1 — Comment out the auto-detect line. This line already exists in the file by default. Find it and put a # in front of it to disable it:

#camera_auto_detect=1

Step 2 — Add the OV5647 driver line. This line does not exist yet. Type it in on a new line:

dtoverlay=ov5647

After both changes, the bottom of your config.txt should look exactly like this:

#camera_auto_detect=1
dtoverlay=ov5647

Save and exit: Ctrl+O → Enter → Ctrl+X

Then reboot:

sudo reboot

Skip this = 'no cameras available' error every time

This step is mandatory regardless of what software you install.

docs.title: Phase 2: Install Build Dependencies
docs.text:
Update the system:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

Install build tools and required libraries:

sudo apt install -y git ninja-build pkg-config libepoxy-dev libjpeg-dev libtiff5-dev \
libpng-dev libboost-dev libboost-program-options-dev libdrm-dev libexif-dev \
python3-pip python3-jinja2 python3-yaml python3-ply libgnutls28-dev openssl libssl-dev

Remove the old Meson:

sudo apt remove -y meson

Install the latest Meson via pip:

sudo pip3 install meson

Clear the shell command cache so it picks up the new Meson:

hash -r

Why upgrade Meson?

Ubuntu 22.04 ships an old Meson version that can't handle new libcamera build scripts. pip3 install meson gets the latest. hash -r clears the shell cache so it picks up the new one.

docs.title: Phase 3: Build libcamera from Source
docs.text:
Ubuntu's default libcamera package is incompatible with the Pi's camera stack. Building from source gives you proper hardware optimization.

Clone the repository:

cd ~
git clone https://git.libcamera.org/libcamera/libcamera.git
cd libcamera

Configure for Raspberry Pi 4 (vc4 pipeline):

meson setup build -Dpipelines=rpi/vc4 -Dipas=rpi/vc4 -Dv4l2=enabled \
-Dgstreamer=disabled -Dtest=false -Dlc-compliance=disabled -Dcam=disabled \
-Dqcam=disabled -Ddocumentation=disabled -Dprefix=/usr

Compile:

ninja -C build

Install:

sudo ninja -C build install

Refresh the shared library cache:

sudo ldconfig

docs.title: Phase 4: Build rpicam-apps from Source
docs.text:
These are the actual commands (rpicam-jpeg, rpicam-vid) you use to interact with the camera.

Clone the repository:

cd ~
git clone https://github.com/raspberrypi/rpicam-apps.git
cd rpicam-apps

Configure for headless Ubuntu (no GUI dependencies):

meson setup build -Denable_libav=disabled -Denable_drm=enabled \
-Denable_egl=disabled -Denable_qt=disabled -Denable_opencv=disabled

Compile:

ninja -C build

Install:

sudo ninja -C build install

Refresh the shared library cache:

sudo ldconfig

docs.title: Phase 5: Capturing Media
docs.text:
Capture a photo:

rpicam-jpeg -o lab_photo.jpg

Record a 10-second video:

rpicam-vid -t 10000 -o lab_video.h264

Convert to MP4 (needed for browser playback — .h264 won't play directly):

ffmpeg -framerate 30 -i lab_video.h264 -c copy lab_video.mp4

docs.title: Phase 6: Viewing Files Remotely
docs.text:
Start a simple HTTP server in the folder where your files are saved:

python3 -m http.server 8000

Then open your laptop's browser and go to:

http://<your_pi_ip>:8000
  • Click lab_photo.jpg to view the photo
  • Click lab_video.mp4 to play the video

docs.title: Phase 7: Live Streaming
docs.text:
Method A — Desktop Window (on Pi's GUI)Method B — Stream to Laptop via VLC (Low Latency)

Run this inside the Pi's desktop terminal (via monitor or Remote Desktop):

rpicam-vid -t 0 --inline -o - | ffplay -window_title "Live Feed" -i -

On the Pi:

rpicam-vid -t 0 --inline --listen -o tcp://0.0.0.0:8888

On your laptop — open VLC, press Ctrl+N and enter:

tcp/h264://your_pi_ip:8888

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Task Command Capture photo rpicam-jpeg -o test.jpg Record video rpicam-vid -t 10000 -o test.h264 Convert to MP4 ffmpeg -framerate 30 -i test.h264 -c copy test.mp4 View files remotely python3 -m http.server 8000 Live stream (desktop) rpicam-vid -t 0 --inline -o - \| ffplay -i - Live stream (VLC) rpicam-vid -t 0 --inline --listen -o tcp://0.0.0.0:8888

docs.title: Why This All Works
docs.text: Fix Reason dtoverlay=ov5647 Stops the Pi guessing and loads the exact Rev 1.3 driver Meson upgrade Old Ubuntu version couldn't parse new libcamera build scripts Building libcamera from source Ubuntu's packaged version lacks Pi-specific hardware optimizations Boost libraries C++ dependencies that let rpicam-apps handle your inputs correctly

docs.title: Headless Raspberry Pi Deployment Guide
docs.text:
Why this guide exists

The standard Ubuntu Desktop is not "remotely friendly" by default. The Server version is a clean slate you can control. Headless troubleshooting is a huge part of working with servers and IoT as a CSE student.

docs.title: Phase 1: The Imager (Pre-Boot)
docs.text:
Do NOT choose Ubuntu Desktop

Choose Ubuntu Server 22.04 LTS (64-bit) when flashing. The Desktop version will cause headless issues later.

  1. Click Next and select Edit Settings.

  2. General Tab — fill in:

    • Hostname (e.g., sparkplug)
    • Username and password
    • Your exact Wi-Fi SSID and password

  3. Services Tab — check Enable SSH and select Use password authentication.

  4. Click Write to flash the image.

docs.title: Phase 2: Initial Access & Updates
docs.text:
Once the Pi boots, find its IP address using a network scanner, then:

1. SSH into the Pi:

ssh username@your_ip_address

2. Update the system — this is CRITICAL:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

docs.title: Phase 3: The "Stable Desktop" Stack
docs.text:
The default Ubuntu GNOME desktop crashes on headless setups because it needs a physical monitor to stay stable. The solution is XFCE4 — lightweight, fast, and monitor-independent.

Run these commands in order:

1. Install the desktop environment and the remote server:

sudo apt install xfce4 xfce4-goodies xrdp -y

Note

If a purple screen appears during install, press Tab to highlight OK and hit Enter.

2. Add your user to the security group:

sudo adduser your_username ssl-cert

3. Configure the desktop identity — fixes the "auto-closing window" bug:

echo "xfce4-session" > ~/.xsession

4. The "Headless Permission" fix:

sudo sh -c 'echo "allowed_users=anybody" > /etc/X11/Xwrapper.config'

5. The "Double-Login / Crash" fix:

Open the startup script:

sudo nano /etc/xrdp/startwm.sh

Scroll to the bottom and paste these two lines above the last test and exec lines:

unset DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS
unset XDG_RUNTIME_DIR

Save and exit: Ctrl+O → Enter → Ctrl+X

6. Restart the XRDP service:

sudo systemctl restart xrdp

docs.title: Phase 4: Connecting from Windows
docs.text:
1. Open Remote Desktop Connection on Windows.
  2. Enter the Pi's IP address.
  3. Log in with your username and password.

docs.title: Why This Works
docs.text:
Component Reason Ubuntu Server Lets you inject Wi-Fi and SSH settings before the Pi even turns on XFCE4 GNOME crashes without a physical monitor — XFCE doesn't care .xsession file Acts as a signpost, telling Remote Desktop which desktop environment to launch on login startwm.sh edit Clears conflicting session variables that cause crashes or double-login loops Xwrapper.config Grants permission for any user to start an X display without a physical screen

You're ready!

You can now use your laptop screen, keyboard, and mouse to build Django backends, React frontends, or Machine Learning models directly on the Pi — no monitor needed.

docs.title: USB Webcam Setup on Ubuntu 22.04 LTS
docs.text:
Context

Unlike the Pi Camera, USB webcams require no firmware edits, no custom compiles, and no driver installation. They use the Linux kernel's built-in Universal Video Class (UVC) drivers — plug in and go.

Pi Camera + USB Camera = No Conflict

Because they use completely different pathways in the OS, you can run both cameras at the exact same time without any conflicts. The Pi Camera uses the internal ISP and libcamera stack, while the USB camera bypasses all of that entirely.

docs.title: Phase 1: Verify the Camera is Recognized
docs.text:
Check the USB bus — confirm your camera appears:

lsusb

Find the video device node:

ls -l /dev/video*

Which /dev/video node is yours?

If the Pi Camera is active, it usually claims /dev/video0. Your USB camera will likely register as /dev/video1 or /dev/video2. Take note of the node number — you'll need it in every command below.

docs.title: Phase 2: Install Required Tools
docs.text:
USB cameras process their own images internally, so you need standard Linux video tools — not rpicam-apps.

Update the system:

sudo apt update

Install the tools:

sudo apt install -y fswebcam ffmpeg v4l-utils
Tool Purpose fswebcam Captures still photos from a USB camera ffmpeg Records video from a USB camera v4l-utils Video4Linux utilities — inspect and manage video devices

docs.title: Phase 3: Capturing Media
docs.text:
Check your device node first

The commands below use /dev/video1 as an example. Replace it with whatever node your camera registered as in Phase 1.

Capture a photo:

fswebcam -d /dev/video1 -r 1280x720 --no-banner usb_photo.jpg

Record a video:

ffmpeg -f v4l2 -framerate 30 -video_size 1280x720 -i /dev/video1 output_usb.mp4

docs.title: Phase 4: Viewing Files Remotely
docs.text:
Start an HTTP server in the folder where your files are saved:

python3 -m http.server 8000

Then open your laptop's browser and go to:

http://<your_pi_ip>:8000
  • Click usb_photo.jpg to view the photo
  • Click output_usb.mp4 to play the video

docs.title: Why This Works So Easily
docs.text: Reason Explanation Built-in UVC Drivers The Linux kernel natively understands the processors inside USB cameras — no manual driver setup needed Hardware Independence The USB pathway completely bypasses the Pi's internal ISP and the custom libcamera stack you built for the Pi Camera Simultaneous Operation Pi Camera and USB Camera use different OS pathways — they can run at the same time with zero conflicts

docs.title: YOLOv11 Edge AI on Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
What this guide covers

A complete pipeline from a blank Raspberry Pi to a high-speed, edge-optimized YOLOv11 object tracker — with dedicated branches for both the Pi Camera (ribbon cable) and USB Webcam.

docs.title: Phase 1: Clean Room Environment
docs.text:
Always build inside an isolated virtual environment so Ubuntu doesn't accidentally pull in broken server-grade NVIDIA packages.

Create and enter the project folder:

mkdir -p ~/yolo && cd ~/yolo

Create the virtual environment:

python3 -m venv venv

Activate it:

source venv/bin/activate

Install Pi-Safe (CPU Only) PyTorch:

pip install torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu

Install YOLO and NCNN:

pip install ultralytics ncnn

docs.title: Phase 2: Hardware Crash Prevention
docs.text:
Do this before running anything

By default, the math library OpenBLAS will panic and throw an Illegal instruction (core dumped) error because it doesn't recognize the Pi's CPU architecture. This fix is permanent and survives reboots.

Apply the permanent fix:

echo 'export OPENBLAS_CORETYPE=ARMV8' >> ~/.bashrc

Reload your shell so it takes effect immediately:

source ~/.bashrc

docs.title: Phase 3: Export to NCNN Format
docs.text:
The standard PyTorch .pt file is too heavy for the Pi. You must convert it to NCNN — an ultra-fast, C++ optimized format built for edge devices.

Make sure your venv is active before running this

Run the export:

python3 -c "from ultralytics import YOLO; YOLO('yolo11n.pt').export(format='ncnn')"

Wait 1–3 minutes. When complete, you will see a yolo11n_ncnn_model/ folder generated in your directory.

docs.title: Phase 4: Camera Scripts
docs.text:
Both scripts use two key optimizations:

Optimization Reason imgsz=320 Halves the input resolution → roughly doubles FPS on the Pi FOURCC=YUYV Forces standard color format → prevents OpenCV reshape crashes 📷 Pi Camera (Ribbon Cable)🔌 USB Webcam

Create the script:

nano ~/yolo/pi_cam_yolo.py

Paste this code:

import cv2
from ultralytics import YOLO
import time

print("[INFO] Loading NCNN Edge model...")
model = YOLO("yolo11n_ncnn_model", task="detect")

print("[INFO] Opening Pi Camera (requires libcamerify)...")
cap = cv2.VideoCapture(0, cv2.CAP_V4L2)

# Force YUYV to prevent OpenCV reshape crashes
cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FOURCC, cv2.VideoWriter_fourcc(*'YUYV'))
cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_WIDTH, 640)
cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_HEIGHT, 480)

if not cap.isOpened():
    print("[ERROR] Cannot open Pi Camera. Did you use libcamerify?")
    exit(1)

fps = 0
while True:
    ret, frame = cap.read()
    if not ret or frame is None:
        time.sleep(0.1)
        continue

    # imgsz=320 doubles your FPS!
    t0 = time.time()

    results = model(frame, verbose=False)[0]
    # results = model(frame, imgsz=320, verbose=False)[0]

    inf_ms = (time.time() - t0) * 1000
    fps = fps * 0.8 + 0.2 * (1000.0 / max(inf_ms, 1.0))

    annotated = results.plot()
    cv2.putText(annotated, f"Pi Cam FPS: {fps:.1f}", (10, 30),
                cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX, 1.0, (0, 255, 0), 2)
    cv2.imshow("Pi Camera YOLO Stream", annotated)

    # Listen for keyboard presses
    key = cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF

    if key == ord('q'):
        # Press 'q' to quit
        break
    elif key == ord('p'):
        # Press 'p' to take a picture!
        timestamp = int(time.time())
        filename = f"snapshot_{timestamp}.jpg"
        cv2.imwrite(filename, annotated)
        print(f"[SNAP!] Picture saved as: {filename}")

cap.release()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

Create the script:

nano ~/yolo/usb_webcam_yolo.py

Paste this code:

import cv2
from ultralytics import YOLO
import time

print("[INFO] Loading NCNN Edge model...")
model = YOLO("yolo11n_ncnn_model", task="detect")

print("[INFO] Opening USB Webcam natively...")
# Change index to 0 if the USB cam is the ONLY camera plugged in
cap = cv2.VideoCapture(1, cv2.CAP_V4L2)

cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FOURCC, cv2.VideoWriter_fourcc(*'YUYV'))
cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_WIDTH, 640)
cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_HEIGHT, 480)

if not cap.isOpened():
    print("[ERROR] Cannot open USB Camera. Try changing the index to 0 or 2.")
    exit(1)

fps = 0
while True:
    ret, frame = cap.read()
    if not ret or frame is None:
        time.sleep(0.1)
        continue

    t0 = time.time()

    results = model(frame, verbose=False)[0]
    # results = model(frame, imgsz=320, verbose=False)[0]

    inf_ms = (time.time() - t0) * 1000
    fps = fps * 0.8 + 0.2 * (1000.0 / max(inf_ms, 1.0))

    annotated = results.plot()
    cv2.putText(annotated, f"USB Cam FPS: {fps:.1f}", (10, 30),
                cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX, 1.0, (255, 0, 0), 2)
    cv2.imshow("USB Webcam YOLO Stream", annotated)

    # Listen for keyboard presses
    key = cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF

    if key == ord('q'):
        # Press 'q' to quit
        break
    elif key == ord('p'):
        # Press 'p' to take a picture!
        timestamp = int(time.time())
        filename = f"snapshot_{timestamp}.jpg"
        cv2.imwrite(filename, annotated)
        print(f"[SNAP!] Picture saved as: {filename}")

cap.release()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

docs.title: Phase 5: Launch Commands
docs.text:
Activate your venv first

Always run source venv/bin/activate before launching any script.

📷 Pi Camera🔌 USB Webcam

You must use the libcamerify wrapper so OpenCV can understand the ribbon cable:

libcamerify python3 pi_cam_yolo.py

Do not use the wrapper. USB is natively understood by Linux:

python3 usb_webcam_yolo.py

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Error Fix "Camera index out of range" or "Not a video capture device" A previous script crashed and locked the hardware. Run sudo killall python3 "Illegal instruction (core dumped)" The terminal forgot your CPU architecture. Run export OPENBLAS_CORETYPE=ARMV8 "Bad new number of rows in function 'reshape'" Camera is sending raw sensor data. Ensure cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FOURCC, cv2.VideoWriter_fourcc(*'YUYV')) is in your script Can't find the USB Webcam index Run v4l2-ctl --list-devices to see exactly which /dev/videoX it was assigned

docs.title: Recursion
docs.text:
Recursion is when a function calls itself repeatedly.

Always have a Base Case

Without a base case, the function will call itself forever and crash.

# prints n down to 1

    if n == 0:       # base case — stops the recursion
        return
    print(n)
    show(n - 1)      # recursive call

A set is a collection of unordered, unique elements.

docs.title: Classes & Objects
docs.text:
OOP maps real-world scenarios into code using objects.

Term Meaning Class Blueprint for creating objects Object An instance of a class

docs.title: Basic Class & Object
docs.text:
class Student:
    name = "karan kumar"    # class attribute

s1 = Student()              # create object (instance)
print(s1.name)

docs.title: __init__ Constructor
docs.text:
The __init__() method runs automatically whenever a class is instantiated. Used to set object attributes.

class Student:
    college = "ABC College"     # class attribute — shared by ALL objects

    def __init__(self, fullname):
        self.name = fullname    # object attribute — unique per object

s1 = Student("karan")
print(s1.name)

self

self is a reference to the current instance of the class. It's how you access variables that belong to the object.

Object attr > Class attr

If an object attribute has the same name as a class attribute, the object attribute takes priority.

docs.title: Encapsulation
docs.text: Encapsulation means wrapping data and functions into a single unit (object), and controlling access to them.

docs.title: Private Attributes & Methods
docs.text:
Use a __ (double underscore) prefix to make attributes or methods private — accessible only within the class.

class Account:
    def __init__(self, acc_no, acc_pass):
        self.acc_no = acc_no
        self.__acc_pass = acc_pass      # private attribute

    def __sayHello(self):               # private method
        print("hello")

    def welcome(self):
        self.__sayHello()               # ✅ can call private method inside class

docs.title: Access Rules
docs.text:
acc1 = Account("12345", "abcde")

print(acc1.acc_no)          # ✅ works — public attribute
print(acc1.__acc_pass)      # ❌ AttributeError — private, can't access outside
acc1.__sayHello()           # ❌ AttributeError — private, can't call outside
acc1.welcome()              # ✅ works — public method that calls private method internally

docs.title: The 4 Pillars of OOP
docs.text: Pillar Description Abstraction Hide implementation details — show only essential features to the user Encapsulation Wrap data and functions into a single unit (object) Inheritance A child class derives properties & methods from a parent class Polymorphism Same operator/function behaves differently based on context

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text:
When a child/derived class inherits the properties and methods of a parent/base class.

class Car:
    pass

class Toyota(Car):      # Toyota inherits from Car
    pass

docs.title: Types of Inheritance
docs.text:
• Single Inheritance — one child, one parent
  • Multi-level Inheritance — child → parent → grandparent
  • Multiple Inheritance — one child, multiple parents

docs.title: super() Method
docs.text:
Used to access methods of the parent class from within the child class.

class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

class Dog(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        super().__init__(name)    # calls Animal's __init__
        self.breed = breed

docs.title: Polymorphism: Operator Overloading
docs.text:
The same operator can behave differently depending on the types involved. Python uses dunder (double underscore) methods under the hood.

Expression Operation Dunder Method a + b Addition a.__add__(b) a - b Subtraction a.__sub__(b) a * b Multiplication a.__mul__(b) a / b Division a.__truediv__(b) a % b Modulus a.__mod__(b)

Learn More

Visit Python Data Model — Section 3.3.8 for the full list of dunder methods.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: Methods are functions that belong to objects.

docs.title: Instance Methods
docs.text:
Use self to access the object's attributes.

class Student:
    def __init__(self, fullname):
        self.name = fullname

    def hello(self):
        print("hello", self.name)

s1 = Student("karan")
s1.hello()

docs.title: Static Methods
docs.text:
Methods that don't use self — work at the class level, not the instance level.

class Student:
    @staticmethod           # decorator
    def college():
        print("ABC College")

Decorators

Decorators wrap a function to extend its behavior without permanently modifying it.

docs.title: Class Methods
docs.text:
Bound to the class itself, not to an instance. Receives cls (the class) as the first argument.

class Person:
    name = "anonymous"

    @classmethod
    def changeName(cls, name):
        cls.name = name

p1 = Person()
p1.changeName("rahul kumar")
print(p1.name)      # "rahul kumar"
print(Person.name)  # "rahul kumar"

docs.title: Summary: 3 Types of Methods
docs.text: Type Decorator First Parameter Access Instance? Access Class? Instance method — self ✅ ✅ Class method @classmethod cls ❌ ✅ Static method @staticmethod — ❌ ❌

docs.title: del Keyword
docs.text:
del s1.name     # deletes a specific attribute
del s1          # deletes the entire object

docs.title: Property Decorator
docs.text:
Use @property to access a method like an attribute (getter).

class Student:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.__name = name

    @property
    def name(self):
        return self.__name

s1 = Student("karan")
print(s1.name)      # accessed like an attribute, not s1.name()

Also available: @name.setter and @name.deleter decorators.

docs.title: Git & GitHub — Complete Beginner Notes
docs.text:
A practical note for learning Git from the beginning.

The goal of this note is not only to memorize commands, but to understand what Git is doing, why we use each command, and how Git and GitHub work together.

docs.title: 1. What is Git?
docs.text:
Git is a version control system.

Version control means:

Git keeps track of changes made to our files over time.

For example, suppose we have:

project/
├── index.html
├── style.css
└── script.js

Today everything works.

Tomorrow we change script.js and something breaks.

Without Git, we may have to remember what we changed.

With Git, we can see:

  • what changed
  • when it changed
  • who changed it
  • previous versions of the project
  • which changes belong to which version

So Git is basically a system for tracking the history of a project.

docs.title: 2. Git vs GitHub
docs.text: This is one of the most important things to understand.

docs.title: Git
docs.text:
Git is the actual version control software running on our computer.

We use commands like:

git init
git add
git commit
git branch
git merge

Git can work completely without GitHub.

docs.title: GitHub
docs.text:
GitHub is an online platform where Git repositories can be stored and shared.

So:

Git
↓
works on our computer

GitHub
↓
stores/shares Git repositories online

Git is the tool.

GitHub is an online service that works with Git repositories.

docs.title: 3. Why Do We Need Git?
docs.text:
Imagine we are developing a project.

At different times, we might have:

project-final
project-final-2
project-final-new
project-final-new-real
project-final-new-real-2

This becomes difficult to manage.

Git solves this problem.

Instead of making many copies, Git stores the history:

Version 1
   ↓
Version 2
   ↓
Version 3
   ↓
Version 4

We can move through the project's history when necessary.

docs.title: 4. Install Git
docs.text:
First install Git on the computer.

After installation, Git commands become available in the terminal.

On Windows, Git Bash is also commonly installed with Git.

docs.title: 5. Check Git Installation
docs.text:
Open a terminal and run:

git --version

Example:

git version 2.x.x

If a version appears, Git is installed.

docs.title: 6. Git Configuration
docs.text:
Before making commits, we normally configure our name and email.

git config --global user.name "Your Name"

Example:

git config --global user.name "Tanim"

Set email:

git config --global user.email "your-email@example.com"

Check the configuration:

git config --global --list

docs.title: Why do we need this?
docs.text:
Every commit has information about the person who created it.

So Git records:

Author: Tanim
Email: your-email@example.com

docs.title: 7. Git's Basic Idea
docs.text:
The most important Git concept is:

Working Directory
       ↓
   git add
       ↓
Staging Area
       ↓
 git commit
       ↓
Git Repository

We should understand this before memorizing commands.

docs.title: 8. Create a Git Repository
docs.text:
Suppose we have a project:

my-project/
├── index.html
├── style.css
└── script.js

Open the terminal inside the project folder.

Run:

git init

Git will create a hidden .git directory.

Conceptually:

my-project/
├── .git/
├── index.html
├── style.css
└── script.js

The .git directory contains Git's internal repository information and history.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Do not manually edit or delete .git.

If .git is deleted, that local Git repository's history/configuration is removed from that folder.

docs.title: 9. git status
docs.text:
This is one of the commands we will use most often.

git status

It tells us the current state of the repository.

For example:

On branch main

Untracked files:
  index.html
  style.css

This means Git sees the files, but they are not currently being tracked.

docs.title: Very useful habit
docs.text:
When confused, run:

git status

It often tells us what is happening and what Git expects next.

docs.title: 10. The Three Important Areas
docs.text: Git can be understood using three main areas.

docs.title: 1. Working Directory
docs.text:
This is the actual project files we edit.

Example:

index.html
script.js
style.css

docs.title: 2. Staging Area
docs.text:
This is where we prepare changes that should go into the next commit.

We use:

git add

docs.title: 3. Repository
docs.text:
This contains committed history.

We use:

git commit

So:

Edit files
   ↓
Working Directory
   ↓
git add
   ↓
Staging Area
   ↓
git commit
   ↓
Repository

docs.title: 11. git add
docs.text:
Suppose we changed script.js.

Check:

git status

Then:

git add script.js

Now the change is staged.

Check again:

git status

Git will show that script.js is ready to be committed.

docs.title: Add multiple files
docs.text: git add index.html style.css script.js

docs.title: Add everything
docs.text:
git add .

This stages changes in the current directory and its subdirectories.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
git add . does not mean "save the project permanently".

It only prepares the changes for the next commit.

docs.title: 12. git commit
docs.text:
After staging the changes:

git commit -m "Add homepage"

A commit is a saved point in the Git history.

For example:

commit 1
"Create project"

commit 2
"Add navigation"

commit 3
"Fix navbar"

commit 4
"Add TypeScript notes"

The message should describe what the commit does.

Good:

git commit -m "Add TypeScript notes"

Good:

git commit -m "Fix navigation links"

Less useful:

git commit -m "update"

docs.title: 13. The Basic Git Workflow
docs.text: This is the workflow we will use again and again.

docs.title: Step 1 — Change files
docs.text: Edit the project normally.

docs.title: Step 2 — Check what changed
docs.text: git status

docs.title: Step 3 — Stage the changes
docs.text: git add .

docs.title: Step 4 — Commit
docs.text:
git commit -m "Describe the changes"

So the basic workflow is:

Edit
 ↓
git status
 ↓
git add .
 ↓
git commit -m "message"

If the project is connected to GitHub, there is usually another step:

git push

So:

Edit
 ↓
git status
 ↓
git add .
 ↓
git commit
 ↓
git push
 ↓
GitHub

docs.title: 14. git log
docs.text:
To see commit history:

git log

Example:

commit abc123...
Author: Tanim
Date: ...

    Add TypeScript notes

commit def456...
Author: Tanim
Date: ...

    Add JavaScript notes

A shorter version:

git log --oneline

Example:

abc1234 Add TypeScript notes
def4567 Add JavaScript notes
123abcd Create website

This is much easier to read.

docs.title: 15. git diff
docs.text:
git diff shows changes that have not been staged yet.

Suppose we change:

console.log("Hello")

to:

console.log("Hello World")

Run:

git diff

Git shows what changed.

This is useful before running:

git add .

because we can inspect our changes first.

docs.title: Difference between status and diff
docs.text:
git status

tells us which files changed and their Git state.

git diff

shows the actual content changes.

docs.title: 16. Working with Multiple Files
docs.text:
Suppose we changed:

index.html
style.css
script.js

We can stage all:

git add .

Then:

git commit -m "Update website"

But sometimes we only want some changes.

For example:

git add index.html

Then only index.html is staged.

This is useful when changes belong to different tasks.

docs.title: 17. The .gitignore File
docs.text:
Some files should not be uploaded to Git.

Examples:

node_modules/
.env
dist/

We can create:

.gitignore

Example:

node_modules/
.env
dist/

Now Git will ignore those paths when deciding what untracked files to report.

docs.title: Why ignore node_modules?
docs.text:
Node projects can contain thousands of installed dependency files.

Instead of uploading the entire node_modules folder, we normally keep the dependency information in files such as:

package.json
package-lock.json

Then another developer can install dependencies with:

npm install

docs.title: Why ignore .env?
docs.text:
.env files may contain secrets such as:

API_KEY=...
DATABASE_PASSWORD=...

We should not accidentally publish secrets to GitHub.

docs.title: 18. Branches
docs.text:
A branch allows us to work on a separate line of development.

Suppose our main project is:

main

We want to add a new feature.

Instead of directly changing main, we can create:

feature/navbar

Now:

main
  \
   feature/navbar

We work on the feature branch.

After the feature is finished, we can merge it back into main.

docs.title: 19. Create and Switch Branches
docs.text:
See current branch:

git branch

Create a branch:

git branch feature-navbar

Switch to it:

git switch feature-navbar

A convenient command creates and switches at the same time:

git switch -c feature-navbar

Now we are working on:

feature-navbar

docs.title: Older command
docs.text:
You may also see:

git checkout -b feature-navbar

This is still widely encountered.

For learning the newer workflow, git switch is easier to understand because it is specifically designed for branch switching.

docs.title: 20. Merge
docs.text:
Suppose we have:

main
feature-navbar

We finished the feature.

First switch to main:

git switch main

Then merge:

git merge feature-navbar

Conceptually:

feature-navbar
       \
        → main

The changes from the feature branch are brought into main.

docs.title: 21. Merge Conflicts
docs.text:
Sometimes Git cannot automatically merge two changes.

Example:

On one branch:

const title = "Hello";

Another branch changes the same line to:

const title = "Hello World";

Git may not know which version should win.

This creates a merge conflict.

Git may mark the file like:

<<<<<<< HEAD
const title = "Hello";
=======
const title = "Hello World";
>>>>>>> feature-navbar

We manually decide which code should remain.

Then:

git add .

and create the merge commit if Git requires one:

git commit

docs.title: Important idea
docs.text:
A merge conflict is not necessarily an error in Git.

It means:

Git needs a human to decide which conflicting change should remain.

docs.title: 22. Remote Repository
docs.text:
Until now we have mostly talked about Git on our computer.

A remote repository is another Git repository, usually hosted somewhere online.

For example:

Local repository
       ↓
   Internet
       ↓
Remote repository

GitHub is a common place to host the remote repository.

docs.title: 23. GitHub
docs.text:
GitHub allows us to:

  • store Git repositories online
  • collaborate with other developers
  • review code
  • create pull requests
  • manage issues
  • publish websites
  • keep a backup of our repository

A common setup is:

Your computer
   ↓
Local Git repository
   ↓
GitHub
   ↓
Remote Git repository

docs.title: 24. git remote
docs.text:
To see configured remote repositories:

git remote -v

Example:

origin  https://github.com/username/project.git (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/username/project.git (push)

Usually the remote is named:

origin

origin is just a conventional name.

It is not a special requirement that the remote must be called origin.

docs.title: Add a remote
docs.text:
git remote add origin https://github.com/username/project.git

Check:

git remote -v

docs.title: 25. git clone
docs.text:
Suppose a project already exists on GitHub.

We want to download the repository to our computer.

Use:

git clone https://github.com/username/project.git

Git will:

  • download the repository
  • create a local project directory
  • bring the Git history
  • configure the remote repository

Then:

cd project

docs.title: 26. git push
docs.text:
git push sends local commits to a remote repository.

Example:

git push

For the first push of a new branch, we may use:

git push -u origin main

The -u option sets the upstream relationship so future pushes can usually be shorter:

git push

docs.title: 27. git pull
docs.text:
git pull brings changes from the remote repository into the current local branch.

Example:

git pull

Conceptually:

GitHub
  ↓
git pull
  ↓
Your local repository

This is useful when the remote repository has changes that your local repository does not have.

docs.title: 28. git fetch
docs.text:
git fetch downloads information about changes from the remote repository without automatically merging those changes into the current branch.

git fetch

Conceptually:

GitHub
  ↓
git fetch
  ↓
Local Git knows about remote changes

But your current working branch is not automatically updated by the fetch itself.

This makes fetch useful when we want to inspect remote changes before deciding what to do.

docs.title: 29. Clone vs Pull
docs.text: These are commonly confused.

docs.title: git clone
docs.text:
Used when we do not have the repository locally yet.

git clone URL

Think:

"Give me this repository for the first time."

docs.title: git pull
docs.text:
Used when we already have a local copy and want newer remote changes.

git pull

Think:

"Update my existing local repository."

docs.title: 30. Fork
docs.text:
A fork is a GitHub feature.

Suppose another developer has a repository and we want our own GitHub copy of it.

We can fork it.

Conceptually:

Other person's repository
          ↓
        Fork
          ↓
Your GitHub repository

A fork is especially useful when contributing to projects where we do not have direct write access.

docs.title: 31. Pull Request
docs.text:
A Pull Request (PR) is a request to merge changes from one branch/repository into another.

Typical workflow:

Fork repository
      ↓
Clone repository
      ↓
Create branch
      ↓
Make changes
      ↓
Commit
      ↓
Push branch
      ↓
Create Pull Request
      ↓
Review
      ↓
Merge

Pull Requests are heavily used in collaborative development.

docs.title: 32. git restore
docs.text:
Sometimes we change a file but decide we do not want those changes.

Suppose:

script.js

was modified.

We can restore the working-tree version from the last recorded state:

git restore script.js

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
This discards the uncommitted changes in that file.

So be careful.

Do not use it on changes you may still need.

docs.title: Unstage a file
docs.text:
Suppose we ran:

git add script.js

but we do not want it staged anymore.

Use:

git restore --staged script.js

This removes the file from the staging area but keeps the changes in the working directory.

docs.title: 33. git reset
docs.text:
git reset can move the current branch's history pointer and/or change staging state.

Because it can be destructive, beginners should use it carefully.

A common use is unstaging:

git reset HEAD script.js

This is an older/common form of removing a file from the staging area.

Modern Git documentation often encourages:

git restore --staged script.js

for this specific task.

docs.title: Resetting a commit
docs.text:
You may encounter:

git reset --soft HEAD~1

This moves the branch back one commit while keeping the changes staged.

Another form:

git reset --mixed HEAD~1

moves the branch back one commit and keeps the changes in the working directory but unstaged.

A dangerous form is:

git reset --hard HEAD~1

This can discard changes.

docs.title: Beginner rule
docs.text:
Do not use:

git reset --hard

unless you understand exactly what changes will be removed.

docs.title: 34. git stash
docs.text:
Sometimes we have unfinished work but need to temporarily switch branches.

For example:

You are working on feature A
        ↓
Something urgent needs to be fixed on main
        ↓
But your current work is not ready to commit

We can temporarily store the changes:

git stash

Now the working directory becomes clean.

We can switch branches:

git switch main

After finishing the urgent work, return to the previous branch.

Then restore the stashed changes:

git stash pop

Conceptually:

Unfinished changes
       ↓
   git stash
       ↓
Temporary storage
       ↓
Work somewhere else
       ↓
   git stash pop
       ↓
Changes return

docs.title: 35. git tag
docs.text:
A tag can mark a specific point in Git history.

Tags are commonly used for releases.

Example:

git tag v1.0.0

Then:

git push origin v1.0.0

A project might have:

v1.0.0
v1.1.0
v2.0.0

This makes important versions easy to identify.

docs.title: 36. GitHub Pages and Deployment
docs.text:
GitHub can also host static websites through GitHub Pages.

For example, a repository can contain:

HTML
CSS
JavaScript

and GitHub Pages can publish the site.

For a documentation project such as MkDocs, the workflow can be:

Edit Markdown
      ↓
Build documentation
      ↓
Deploy generated site
      ↓
GitHub Pages
      ↓
Website

docs.title: 37. MkDocs + Git Workflow
docs.text:
For our notes website, we have a project like:

My_Notes/
├── docs/
│   ├── python/
│   ├── javascripts/
│   ├── frameworks/
│   │   └── typescript.md
│   └── index.md
│
├── mkdocs.yml
└── ...

When we add or edit a note:

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text:
Edit the Markdown file.

Example:

docs/frameworks/typescript.md

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text:
Run the local server:

mkdocs serve

This lets us preview the website locally.

Usually the local address looks like:

http://127.0.0.1:8000/

docs.title: Step 3
docs.text:
Check the page.

Make sure:

  • headings work
  • table of contents works
  • code blocks look correct
  • tabs work
  • links work
  • navigation works

docs.title: Step 4
docs.text:
Stop the server:

Ctrl + C

docs.title: Step 5
docs.text:
Build the site:

mkdocs build --strict

This helps detect documentation/configuration problems.

docs.title: Step 6
docs.text:
Commit the changes:

git add .
git commit -m "Add TypeScript notes"

docs.title: Step 7
docs.text:
Push to GitHub:

git push

If the project uses mkdocs gh-deploy for GitHub Pages deployment, the deployment command can be:

mkdocs gh-deploy

The exact deployment command depends on how the repository is configured.

docs.title: 38. A Real Example
docs.text:
Suppose we add:

docs/frameworks/typescript.md

and modify:

mkdocs.yml

First check:

git status

We may see:

modified: mkdocs.yml
untracked: docs/frameworks/typescript.md

Preview:

mkdocs serve

After checking everything:

mkdocs build --strict

Then stage:

git add .

Check:

git status

Commit:

git commit -m "Add TypeScript notes"

Push:

git push

If deployment is done with MkDocs:

mkdocs gh-deploy

Then open the published website.

docs.title: Mistake 1 — Forgetting to commit
docs.text:
Running:

git add .

does not finish the process.

You still need:

git commit -m "message"

docs.title: Mistake 2 — Forgetting to push
docs.text:
A commit is normally local.

If you want that commit on GitHub:

git push

So:

git commit

and:

git push

are not the same thing.

docs.title: Mistake 3 — Thinking git add uploads files
docs.text:
It does not.

git add .

means:

Put these changes into the staging area.

It does not mean:

Upload them to GitHub.

docs.title: Mistake 4 — Thinking Git and GitHub are the same
docs.text:
They are not.

Git      → version control software
GitHub   → online hosting/collaboration platform

docs.title: Mistake 5 — Pushing secrets
docs.text:
Never intentionally commit things like:

.env
API keys
private credentials
passwords

Use .gitignore where appropriate, but remember:

.gitignore does not magically remove a secret that has already been committed.

If a secret has been exposed, it should be treated as compromised and rotated/revoked.

docs.title: Mistake 6 — Using git reset --hard without understanding it
docs.text:
This can discard work.

Always understand what Git is going to remove before using destructive commands.

docs.title: Mistake 7 — Working directly on main for everything
docs.text:
For personal projects, working on main can be completely reasonable.

For larger projects, feature branches are commonly used:

main
 ├── feature-login
 ├── feature-payment
 └── fix-navbar

docs.title: 41. A Simple Mental Model
docs.text:
If you forget everything else, remember this:

                 YOUR COMPUTER
┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                          │
│  Working Directory                       │
│       │                                  │
│       │ git add                          │
│       ↓                                  │
│  Staging Area                            │
│       │                                  │
│       │ git commit                       │
│       ↓                                  │
│  Local Git Repository                    │
│       │                                  │
│       │ git push                         │
└───────┼──────────────────────────────────┘
        ↓
     GITHUB
   Remote Repository

And when someone else has new changes:

GITHUB
   │
   │ git pull
   ↓
YOUR LOCAL REPOSITORY

The core cycle is:

CHANGE
  ↓
STATUS
  ↓
ADD
  ↓
COMMIT
  ↓
PUSH

And when you need other people's changes:

PULL

docs.title: The five commands to learn first
docs.text:
Do not try to memorize every Git command at once.

Start with these:

git status
git add .
git commit -m "message"
git push
git pull

Understand what each one does.

docs.title: The most important difference
docs.text:
git add
    ↓
staging

git commit
    ↓
save a version in local Git history

git push
    ↓
send commits to remote/GitHub

git pull
    ↓
bring remote changes into your local branch

docs.title: A normal daily workflow
docs.text:
git status

# edit files

git status

git add .

git commit -m "Describe what you changed"

git push

If other people are working on the same repository, it is often useful to update your local branch before starting work:

git pull

Then work, commit, and push.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
Git is not something you need to fear.

At the beginning, it may look like there are hundreds of commands. In normal development, however, you repeatedly use a relatively small set of commands.

First become comfortable with:

status
add
commit
push
pull
branch
switch
merge
clone

Once these become familiar, the rest of Git becomes much easier to understand.
